en: In our leisure time from the study of the classics and histories, we have also taken pleasure in dipping our fingers into the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

We do so merely because the text transcribed by Minister Fang is exquisitely crafted and does not contradict the teachings of the orthodox tradition. As for the analysis of mental contemplation and the definitive determination of its fundamental principles, however—
To manifest this for future generations, it would not have been possible without one possessing great faculties and vows.

Surveying the commentaries and sub-commentaries produced since the Tang dynasty, there are no fewer than a hundred or so families of scholars. Some are shallow and fail to reach the mark; others are perverse and contradictory.

Thus, they cannot avoid the lament that the Sūtra remains as obscured as if hidden within a mote of dust. As for those that are most eccentric and egregiously violate the intent of the Sūtra, none surpasses Jiaoguang.
The correct pulse is faint. The *Sūtra* investigates that the awakening mind is the foundation for attaining the Way, yet he says the six consciousnesses are not used.
The *Sūtra* clarifies that the three contemplations are the stages for entering the Way, yet he says the three contemplations are not used.

How is this different from a filial son who, in his self-assurance, beats and throws his parents about and then wishes to have them enter the gate while closing the door? His various errors are manifold; there is no end to them.
These matters can be enumerated. If one examines their origins, they stem from a lack of familiarity with the hidden teachings and a mere arbitrary following of one's own mind.

The Dharma Master Quanzhang of Tiantai attained the true seal of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and held the scales of judgment and interpretation; he expounded upon the contemplation of the mind by means of the categories of the general and the specific.
Thus, the sacred text of ten fascicles is revealed, setting forth the objects of contemplation and the practice of meditation to establish the stages of cultivation and realization;
the essential purport of this single sutra is made manifest, revealing the true permanence through the six consciousnesses and leading toward the fruit of Buddhahood via the three contemplations.
Not only is the long-standing, unresolved case finally settled here, but the erroneous theories of Jiaoguang are also resolved as easily as a blade slicing through wood.
In the past, Jiehuan of Wenling used groundless assertions to falsely obscure the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Master Baisong took up his pen as a battle-axe to clear away its thorns, so that all might joyfully behold the *Lotus Sūtra* once again. Now, Jiaoguang Zhengmai uses his biased and erroneous commentary to defile the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Master Quanzhang grasps his brush like a great beam to execute this rebellion, so that all may compete [in praising] the sūtra.
Beholding the radiance emanating from the Buddha’s crown, it is said that Mencius’s refutation of Yang Zhu and Mo Di was a merit no less than that of Yu the Great.
Is not Master Baesong Chon the true successor who has rendered service to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*?

Indeed, the *Śūraṅgama* was once expounded with such devotion by Master Zixuan of Changshui that he experienced the auspicious omen of falling flowers; now, Master Chon’s definitive understanding has been perfectly realized at this very site.
Could this be the later incarnation of Changshui? Otherwise, how could one possess such power to analyze the contemplation of the mind and resolve a case that remained undecided for a thousand years?
How remarkably clear and well-documented is this work! Nevertheless, because of it, I feel a sense of regret.

This book establishes its principles upon a firm foundation and refutes heterodoxy without reservation; its spirit of luminous integrity and magnanimity overflows with a majestic and awe-inspiring presence.
He was the very embodiment of gentleness and subtle eloquence. As the *Book of Poetry* says, "neither too rigid nor too yielding"—this is precisely how he appeared between pen and tongue.
Had he held this pen while standing at court, he would surely have offered forthright counsel and direct discourse to assist and rectify the sovereign on the throne.

Otherwise, were he to don the embroidered robes to tour the various provinces, he would certainly have buried his carriage wheels in the imperial capital to suppress the violent and eradicate the strong.

Yet in the end, he was taken up as a model by the Buddhists; this is truly a pity. Nevertheless, the laws of the state prohibit people from doing evil, while the Buddha-dharma encourages them toward goodness.
From this day forward, let this work be hung at the gates of the kingdom to turn back perverse attachments and rectify the human heart.
By supporting the royal way and supplementing the teachings of fame and virtue, it will do more than merely continue the legacy of Yu the Great.

How admirable that you long for the far-reaching influence of virtue! Your writings remain intact; there must be those who, upon seeing my words, will sigh with the realization that they have truly found what they sought. At this time.

In the second month of summer in the Gengshen year of the Kangxi era, Zhang Zhen, a native of Changshui, respectfully inscribed this preface for the *Lengyan jing dingjie*. Regarding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*,
ever since I recovered from my illness in the region south of the Ling Mountains, I have devoted myself to its study and translation, and have been praised for it by others on occasion.
I have examined the commentaries and sub-commentaries of various schools;

while their literary elegance is indeed admirable, when one seeks therein a discernment that is precise, a structural arrangement that is exact, and an interpretation that captures the very marrow of Śākyamuni’s intent—encompassing both the initial and subsequent stages of mental cultivation—one finds such instances only rarely.
This spring, Master Quanchang presented me with his *Definitive Explanation of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

This work was composed by fully integrating the principles of the general and specific contemplations of the mind found within the ten chapters of the *Tiantai Zhiguan* (The Great Calming and Contemplation).

Within those ten chapters, only the "Correct Contemplation" addresses the general mind of ignorance, while the "Specific Contemplations" address the minds that attract retribution. Likewise, throughout the ten fascicles of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it too primarily investigates the general mind of ignorance.

The details regarding the minds that attract retribution are distinct; within them, the meanings accord with reason without the slightest discrepancy. The teachings of the Buddha and the admonitions of the Patriarchs are as perfectly joined as two halves of a jade tablet.

Thus, the principle of observing the mind through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is revealed in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, while the discourse on the general and the specific is verified by *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* in the [Mohe] Zhiguan.
It is as if these two sages were conversing hand-in-hand to open the way for a thousand and ten hundred generations.
"This is the swift shortcut for sentient beings to transcend birth and death and realize Bodhi through the contemplation of the mind.
Having read it again and again, I could not help but dance with joy and clap my hands, crying out: 'From this day forward, the heart-spirit, marrow, and bones of Śākyamuni [shall be mine]!'"

He has laid everything out upon the platter, leaving no residue behind. Thus, the wise man’s contemplation of the mind—both in its general and specific aspects—as it manifests in current activity and is attained through realization, is now both credible and evidenced.
It may be said that what was uncertain yesterday is certain today.

Indeed, the illumination of the world by the sūtras and śāstras is like the dragon-sword and its sheath, or the male and female spirits of a separated soul. Prior to Master Quan, these two swords were divided; now they are whole once more.
The souls of the two were united. After Master Quan, the male and female merged and flew away together, singing. This is like the union of a *qiàn* (a type of spirit) and a woman into a single body.
As the Sūtra says: "For example, though a lute, a *sè*, a *pípá*, or a *kōnghóu* may possess exquisite tones, if there are no skilled fingers, they can never produce sound.
Now, the exquisite resonance of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, whose mouths differ yet whose hearts are one, has been brought forth through the union with Master Quan’s skillful fingers.

As for its subtle details and minor points, every character is brought into the contemplation of the mind; preceding calls and subsequent responses, every word is pointed back to the general and the specific.
It is just like a divine dragon in the midst of the sky: when the head moves, the tail responds; with a single breath it soars and circles, leaving no gap whatsoever.

Looking down upon the commentaries and sub-commentaries of other schools, they are all nothing more than gazing at the moon through a gauze screen or guessing at a covered object in the dark—vague and indistinct. How [could they compare]?

How much more so when it comes to the arbitrary views of those who, suspecting the Great Stability (Mahāsamādhi), recklessly deny the Three Contemplations, and who, clinging to the functioning faculties, reject the six consciousnesses—how truly perverse their arguments are!
As for the passages where he provides commentary on the textual phrases, he frequently cites Youxi Jizhong, spanning many pages;
sometimes he connects them with one or two sentences at the beginning, or sometimes he concludes them with one or two characters at the end, ultimately forming [a coherent whole].
Within his entirely impartial mind, he engaged in subtle discourse; there was absolutely no record of me copying his traces.

Furthermore, he caused the phrasing of my old prose to appear even more profound and refined, much like how Wang Mojie added the words "vast and gloomy" (*mo mo yin yin*) to the lines "A white egret flies over the water fields / Yellow orioles warble among the summer trees," thereby perfectly evoking the scene of Wangchuan.
Moreover, he caused my ancient poems to become even more elegant and enduring. Furthermore—
It is like Li Guangbi, who took up the army of Li Ziyi; wherever his commands reached, its spirit and appearance were completely transformed.
This was achieved through true insight, true wisdom, true penmanship, and true learning, thereby accomplishing the method of "seizing the embryo" (transmuting the essence).

It reveals the secrets that not even a thousand sages had opened and settles doubts that have remained unresolved for a thousand autumns. How could this be merely a modern plagiarism of stale clichés?

Is this not like someone gathering door-knobs to invite guests? Should you claim that my praise is exaggerated, please examine the more than one hundred commentaries and sub-commentaries since the translation of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:

has there ever been another work with such precise analysis and exact placement, wherein the beginning and end of the contemplation of mind both capture the very marrow of the Buddhas and Patriarchs with such crystalline clarity?
Written by the Bhikṣu Jinshi Pantan of Mount Danxia on a spring day in the Gengshen year of the Kangxi era.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "How could there be anything spoken by a Śrāvaka? Whatever is spoken is entirely through the power of the Buddha. Indeed.
This interpretation is based on receiving the Buddha’s empowerment and expounding what the Buddha has taught. How could there be anything personally spoken by Lingyao?

Whatever is spoken is likewise nothing other than the teaching of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Śākyamuni taught the methods for contemplating the mind in its general and specific aspects in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*;
the Patriarch Zhiyi taught the methods for contemplating the mind in its general and specific aspects in the *Mohe Zhiguan*. These words may differ in their phrasing...
In brief, though, their ultimate aim is one and the same. The sutra clarifies the path of cultivation through the dharmas of understanding, practice, and realization;

that is, it employs the ten vehicles of sublime contemplation as the primary application of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. This contemplation takes the mind of universal ignorance as its object. The first six chapters of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* follow the *Sūtra*.

To open up wondrous understanding: the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* assembly teaches that the three categories (*triskandha*) and the seven elements (*mahābhūta*) are all fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature (*tathatā-gotra*) of the Tathāgata-garbha.

The *Śūraṅgama*’s "demons of the aggregates" (*skandha-māra*) and the "seven destinies" (*sapta-gati*) correspond precisely to what is excluded in *śamatha-vipaśyanā*: namely, the active manifestations and acquired attainments that can summon retributive minds.

I, Yao, respectfully rely upon the secret empowerment of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to synthesize these two teachings; they are nothing other than the single practice of contemplating the mind (*citta-vipaśyanā*). Thus I have cultivated this work.

After ten years, it was completed in twelve fascicles. This is intended so that those of later generations who are resolved to contemplate the mind may know that the gateway to the nectar of immortality lies herein;

let them no longer discard their cognitive minds or cling to divergent paths and differing doctrines regarding the three contemplations. This is what is called the "Explanation of Contemplating the Mind."

Regarding what is called "fixed" (or definitive), the commentaries and sub-commentaries of the past state in full that the sagely and divine insights of each [master] are correct, yet there is no way to determine which one to follow.

Now, by taking the principle of the Buddhas and Patriarchs’ contemplation of the mind as the standard and reconciling it with the principle of the Buddhas and Patriarchs’ contemplation of the mind, from beginning to end, everything is perfectly integrated, without any superfluous words or redundant meanings.
It seems that even if a thousand sages were to arise again, none could transcend this path. As the *Miaoxuan* says: "The Dharma..."
The "Flower" (Huá) [commentary] is definitive and not indeterminate; this current interpretation likewise refers to that which is definitive and not indeterminate.

As for the extensive discussion of the seven elements (*mahābhūta*) and the threefold distinction between the Perfect and the Separate within the *Xīngzàng* (Nature-Treasury), I have respectfully followed the profound Patriarch [Zhiyi]’s principle of "immediacy within the Middle" (*jìzhōng*).

Nevertheless, I have also interspersed various explanations from Changshui and Tóngzhōu; thus, in the detailed analysis of the text, I have effectively achieved the state of "immediacy within the Middle."
This work abounds in topical divisions and phrases; thus it is called a "Commentary. How could Master Lingyao have anything of his own to say?
Whatever he has said is nothing other than the teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Written respectfully as a preface by the Tiantai bhikṣu Lingyao in the ninth month of the year Wuyin (1681).
The Great Outline of the Contemplation of Mind and its Resolute Understanding from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*— The Definitive Meaning of the Secret Cause, Cultivation,
and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas—
Composed by the Tiantai Bhikṣu Lingyao.

Before providing a definitive interpretation of this sutra, I shall first present its general outline in broad strokes, divided briefly into four chapters: First, distinguishing the general from the specific;
Second, determining the object and the contemplation; Third, explaining the title; Fourth, establishing the conventions.
Regarding the first—distinguishing the general from the specific—it does not mean that the title is the "general" while the sutra text is called the "specific. Rather, it refers to what precedes...

The first seven fascicles of the *Zhengguan* treat the mind of ignorance in its totality to clarify cultivation and realization; the final three fascicles focus on the specific mind that invites retribution to clarify cultivation and realization—these are merely the general and the particular.
Regarding the interpretation of this sutra, more than a hundred and ten schools have offered commentaries, presenting a thousand perspectives that are inconsistent and conflicting.
Some divide the text according to two chapters, some according to five, and some according to six; however, only...
This is because the root source has not yet been cleared and its position remains unsettled; this is how such a definitive understanding is produced, yet one ultimately forgets its own vulgarity.

I humbly maintain that when the Tathāgata appeared in the world and preached this sutra, it was because he wished to show the six classes of ordinary beings how to shatter the obstacles of delusion, karma, and retribution to reveal the wondrous true nature of the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha. It is solely due to...

All sentient beings, within the true nature (*dharmatā*), fail to awaken for even a single thought-moment and thus experience movement. This immediately results in ignorance (*avidyā*) shrouding the enlightened nature.
What is called the ocean of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is eternally abiding, yet it is stirred by the winds of objective realms.

Thus, it becomes obscured and darkened; this is the state of "empty darkness" within the midst of emptiness. This is the obstacle of delusion (*kleśāvaraṇa*), not the obstacle of karmic retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). It is the universal ignorance of the mind, not...

The mind that can summon retribution is an obstruction to principle (*tattva*), not something that draws forth rebirth; it is an affliction of principle (*tattva-kleśa*), not an affliction of phenomena (*vastu-kleśa*);

it is fundamental, not derivative; and it is independent, not associated. Although those in the upper eight stages may temporarily suspend karmic retribution, and although the noble ones of the Three Vehicles may gradually advance to break through the derivative afflictions of phenomena within the three realms, they do not draw forth rebirth into the three existences (*tri-bhava*).
All of these are merely midway stages where ultimate realization has not been attained. This is truly because the fundamental root has not yet been eliminated;
thus, the secret treasury does not manifest and the wondrous nature remains unrevealed.

For this reason, at the assembly on Mount Lengyan, the Buddha set aside the secondary, derivative capacities that correspond to the summoning of retributive results, and instead first demolished the total ignorance (*avidyā*) of the mind—the fundamental obstacle to the principle. Once the fundamental [root]...
Eliminating the branches causes the roots to wither of their own accord; this is the swift method of felling a tree by reaching its root, or cauterizing a disease by hitting its vital point.
Thus, following Ānanda’s request, the Sūtra first establishes the fundamental nature of delusion through successive inquiries as the object to be refuted and observed.
Next, it employs the initial expedient of seven rounds of refuting the "nature" and one shout to refute the "characteristics," thereby revealing *śamatha*.
He then traversed other paths; subsequently, he synthesized the three categories to manifest the myriad phenomena, and by fusing the seven elements, he returned to the Middle Way.
Thus, the wondrous understanding of the secret cause of all Tathāgatas was perfected, and the fundamental Tathāgata-garbha of the Great Buddha-Vertex emerged.

However, this was merely the realization of perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*); if one wishes to initiate cultivation and enter into realization, this alone is not yet sufficient. Therefore—

When the assembly requested entry into the "Flower House" (Huawu), the Tathāgata detailed the fundamental source of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong ben-gen*) and the methods of primary and auxiliary cultivation.
This is because, as it is said, one must rely on a flying ladder to ascend a precipitous ravine; to reach the essential source of truth, one must depend upon wondrous practice.
As for the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi, these are precisely the wondrous fruits cultivated and realized. It is like...
Thus, all the secret causes of the Tathāgatas belong to the definitive meaning (nītārtha), and the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas become ultimately firm and solid.

Even the universal ignorance—the initial single thought of non-awakening that stirs and obscures original awakening—is purified and exhausted without remainder, returning to the state of non-attainment. One should therefore inquire as to the name of this sutra.

It has now entered into circulation. These first seven and a half fascicles of the sutra’s text provide a general outline of the practice by taking the mind of universal ignorance as the primary object of correct contemplation.
As for the aforementioned exposition on the refutation and manifestation of cultivation and realization, this serves to reveal the essence of the Great Buddha-Crown.
It is simply a matter of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) in a single moment of ignorance. Thus, when there is non-awakening in a single thought-moment, there is movement;

once there is movement, there is suffering. Consequently, this spreads like a creeping vine into the ten habitual tendencies associated with the five consciousnesses and the fifth consciousness (the mental consciousness).
These include the shifting flows of the various minds—feeling, perception, and formations—as well as their secondary branches: greed, anger, lust, deceit, and delusion.
Alternatively, these delusions may manifest daily and accumulate karma from time to time; when delusion and karma coincide, they are immediately able to summon retribution.
Once habituation has distanced one from the Single Truth, the resulting retribution summons the seven realms of existence (*sapta-gati*).

This is what is meant by "present activity being able to summon retribution," which refers to the ten causes of habituation in the seventh fascicle. The retribution thus summoned refers to the sixfold mutual retribution in the seventh fascicle. As for this accumulation—
Habitual tendencies form one's nature, and this nature cannot be altered. Whatever one is deeply attached to will manifest throughout successive lifetimes.

Even if one applies the effort of cultivation for a time, there is no way to prevent the frequent emergence of habitual defilements. One may give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*), or to stained craving, or to karmic illnesses, or to views born of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-dṛṣṭi*).
It is like Zhang Sengyou, who was a master painter life after life; he manifested as such even in his rebirths in the Kāñcanamālā world-system.
The old realm consists of the impurities of tomb-keepers and goldsmiths; habitual practice becomes natural, obstructing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and dragging one into saṃsāra.

This constitutes the cause that invites retribution. It is as detailed in the fifty kinds of meditative experiences (*dhyāna-nimitta*) within the *skandha-māra* section from the ninth fascicle onward.
The Sūtra says: "If one does not attain clear awakening, one will be deluded by the *skandhas*."
"You, Ānanda, must be a son of Māra; you have become a person who accomplishes the works of Māra. Furthermore, in this very life, you shall encounter future existence and fall into the Avīci Hell.
The concluding summary regarding the Māra of the five aggregates states: "Each rests within their own cherished, previously habituated deluded mind;

when the karma they have induced comes to an end, they fall into the Avīci Hell. This refers to the retributive fruits thus summoned. These two kinds of mind are merely the branches and the secondary manifestations.
It is not fundamental; it is an obstruction of karma and an obstruction of retribution, not an obstruction of delusion. It is associated [with other mental factors], not independent.

It is the mind that can summon retribution, not the mind of universal ignorance (*avidyā*). It draws forth rebirth, not obstructing the principle. It is a delusion of phenomena (*vastu-moha*), not a delusion of principle (*tattva-moha*).
Since the Buddha has already refuted this single moment of the mind of universal ignorance, realized the three Tathāgata-garbhas, and clarified cultivation and realization, he further...

I pity sentient beings who cling to many peripheral branches and have not yet removed them; thus, when they are in the midst of practicing profound meditative contemplation, their current activities and past habitual tendencies suddenly erupt.
Consequently, the myriad practices of the secret cause cannot penetrate deeply, and the essence of the Great Buddha-Crown cannot attain ultimate firmness.
Therefore, I have minutely investigated the seven destinies to demonstrate how the current manifestation of the ten habitual causes functions.

Regarding the "summoning of retribution": this provides a detailed analysis of the *skandha-māras* (aggregate demons) to refute the arising of habitual tendencies through causal cultivation, which can summon retribution.
One must know that although these two are not fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), they are even more severe obstacles as they harm meditative concentration and lead to rebirth;
therefore, they must be utterly destroyed. Once these two have departed, the Buddha-nature within the crown of my mind will finally attain ultimate realization.
Firm and stable, the secret causes of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas—the myriad practices—are all perfected, and Bodhi returns to non-attainment.
These final three fascicles clarify the matters of cultivation and realization by focusing on the specific mind that can summon retribution.

Within this capacity to summon retribution, there further exist the five consciousnesses of the ten habitual practices and the three minds; through cultivation, the latent seeds of the past are awakened.
The fifty *skandha-māras* are not the same; they ought certainly to be treated in two separate chapters for detailed investigation and refutation. Question:

In the preceding seven fascicles, which concern the general mind of ignorance (*avidyā*), there is refutation, revelation, and the complete and detailed exposition of the methods of practice, realization, and verification.
However, in the final three fascicles, which concern the specific minds that attract retribution, not only are the texts on practice and realization incomplete, but furthermore—
Furthermore, you have not yet refuted Xian’s interpretation. How can you categorize them into two distinct chapters, one general and one specific? Answer:

When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, both detailed and concise expositions are appropriate. Since ignorance is the fundamental obstacle to the principle and its transgression is grave, it ought to be explained in detail to clarify cultivation and realization.
As for the delusions of phenomena that bring about retribution, being merely secondary branches and extremely coarse, it is sufficient to point them out briefly to expose their faults.
If one can remain unattached, one may flow along spontaneously into the state of non-attainment. As it says in the sutras, after the five aggregates have been refuted:

"When the aggregate of consciousness is exhausted, one transcends the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the four stages of application, and the ten grounds, entering the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wondrous adornment.
Is this not the very essence of cultivation and realization, perfectly and clearly present?
The preparatory practices (*saṃbhāra*) and the methods of understanding and practice (*pratipatti*) can be understood by analogy with what precedes; why then list them again and again?

Thus, while the methods of cultivation and realization are explained in detail according to the specific [stages] within the chapter on the "Summary," it is not the case that those exist here while they are absent there.
Whether taken as a whole or individually, entering through any single gate allows one to thoroughly reveal the treasury of nature;

therefore, these two chapters should be presented side by side without any sense of superiority or inferiority. When the Great Master Tiantai expounded the dharma-gates practiced within his own mind, they formed the Ten Chapters of *Zhi Guan*.
Upon seeing this work, a Brahman monk from the Western Regions remarked, "This book is identical to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* of India."

The scriptural passages are identical. Although the Great Master sought scriptural evidence for his treatise but could not find it, I have now recorded the relevant texts from the *Zhi guan fu xing chuan hong jue* (The Commentary on the Practice and Vow of Samatha-Vipaśyanā) and added brief annotations and explanations to harmonize them.

This not only shows that the *Zhi guan* perfectly accords with the subtle excellence of the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*, but also clearly demonstrates that the position of the *Śūraṃgama* within the path of contemplation has a definitive place.
[This is found] in the "Chapter on the Five Superior Stages of Right Cultivation" of the *Zhi guan*.

Having enumerated the ten objects, one first contemplates the object of the aggregates (*skandha*); the remaining nine will be contemplated later. Within the object of the aggregates, there are three different categories.
Since the mind is the root of delusion, if one wishes to investigate, one must strike at its very source. It is like cauterizing a disease: one must hit the correct point.
One should set aside the four aggregates of form and so forth, and contemplate only the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). As for this aggregate of consciousness:

The mind is the sovereign. Thus, the ten modes of contemplation (*daśa-yāna-dhyāna*) are set forth. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) explains: "The mundane and supramundane aggregates (*skandha*) are like branches or diseases;
the single thought-moment of consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*) is like the root or the hollow. If this is so, then contemplating the mind alone should suffice;

why, at the end of the fourth stage, "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas" (*pōfǎ biàn*), does one further apply the contemplation to the remaining aggregates, elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)? Answer: This is intended to harmonize all dharmas and demonstrate that the essence of contemplation is pervasive.

Therefore, the subsequent text uses this as an example for the remaining aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). If one were to demonstrate the essence of the object, contemplating the mind alone would suffice.

Furthermore, when correctly demonstrating the essence of the object, all three—aggregates, elements, and bases—can serve as the basis for contemplation. However, because these are broad and diffuse, they are difficult to enter; thus, we narrow the focus to a specific point.

First, we omit two categories and proceed from the aggregates, like moving from a *zhang* (a measure of ten feet) to a *chi* (a foot). Next, we omit four categories and proceed from consciousness, like moving from a *chi* to an *cun* (an inch). For now, we shall contemplate the mind-king and set aside the others.
Since this concerns mental factors (*caitta*), one first contemplates consciousness (*vijñāna*) and then applies the same principle to the remaining [factors] below. Question:

Both the five sensory consciousnesses and the fivefold mental consciousness can give rise to the three types of mind beginning with feeling (*vedanā*). Which of these consciousnesses and which of the minds they produce constitute the object of contemplation here? Answer:

The five sensory consciousnesses and the fivefold mental consciousness are certainly the objects here, because they have not yet been associated with afflictions and remain in the state of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Among these, one takes [the sixth consciousness]...
That which can attract retribution must still arise through the production [of thought] to belong to the afflictions; other forms of discrimination are what constitute the present object.

Furthermore, although these five consciousnesses and the fifth mental consciousness (manovijñāna) pertain to the present object, they are clarified below in the section on "Traversing Conditions and Facing Objects.

This is found within the sixth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, in the fourth chapter, "The Pervasiveness of the Dharma," which explains śamatha and vipaśyanā by means of the horizontal and vertical aspects of the single mind.
There are two chapters. The first summarizes that the mind of universal ignorance is precisely the mind-king of the aggregates and sense-bases that are being excluded;

that is to say, by taking up this single thought-moment of ignorance, this mind possesses the three truths, which are themselves the three contemplations. The second traces the application of the one mind and the three contemplations to all other phenomena.
If one takes the mind of total ignorance as the object, it may not necessarily be appropriate.

One should further proceed through other single moments of mind—whether a mind of desire, anger, or pride—and when such minds arise, they are likewise empty, provisional, and the Middle, just as explained in the general discussion. Furthermore, it is said:

"What has been explained thus far refers specifically to the contemplation of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); the same applies to the remaining four aggregates. It is likewise for the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*)."

The same applies to the *dhātus*. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), fascicle 28, states: "In observing [the aggregates] as a whole, it is not necessarily appropriate to open up the general to reveal the specific, because within the mind of ignorance (*avidyā*), all other mental states are present.

Answer: Although they are indeed afflictions, they are also subsumed under the categories of wholesome and unwholesome. Furthermore, in this case, one is merely observing the primary minds (*citta-rāja*), such as desire and so forth. If...

This constitutes the textual exposition of the *Zhi guan chuxing chanyi* (The Practice of Stopping and Contemplation). Now, I shall provide a brief commentary and clarification.

In the *Zhi guan*, one selects the realms (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*) to focus specifically on the mind-king within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) and contemplates it using the ten skillful contemplations (*daśayāna*). Once shattered, the contemplation is perfected, one enters into principle, and realizes the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*). This corresponds to the first seven and a half fascicles of the present sutra.

Right contemplation takes the mind of universal ignorance as its object; through the cultivation and realization of clarity, there is both breaking and uniting, leading to awakening, the arousal of practice, and entry onto the true path of Bodhi.

Regarding Yuan Guan’s (Zhiyi) discussion on the "observation of breaking [afflictions]," it is entirely identical to the present sutra’s detailed investigation of the ten habitual causes, such as the seven destinies.

In the *Zhiguan Fuxing* (Subcommentary on the Great Calming and Contemplation), these are termed the "desire-mind," "anger-mind," and "pride-mind"; these are precisely the ten habitual causes of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, namely the habit of greed, the habit of anger, the habit of deception, and so forth.
This is because while the *Mohe Zhiguan* names only the causal minds that attract retribution, the *Śūraṅgama* includes both.
This details the seven realms of rebirth and the sixfold mutual retribution that they summon. As the Sūtra says: "What are the six retributions?
All sentient beings create karma through the six consciousnesses, and the evil retribution summoned thereby issues from the six sense organs.

This specifically indicates that when the consciousnesses correspond with the sense organs and their objects to perform various karmic acts, this is what summons the retribution; the sixfold mutual evil retribution is precisely the retribution thus summoned. [The section on] the Ghosts concludes.
The Master said: "These people all fall due to their pure passions; burned dry by the fires of karma, they emerge above as ghosts.

All such beings are summoned by the karma of their own deluded thoughts. Deluded thought consists of the five consciousnesses, the fifth mental consciousness (manovijñāna), and the three minds of feeling, perception, and volition.
Together with the sense organs and their objects, these conditions create karma, which is what summons the retribution. The realm of ghosts is that which is summoned."

This refers to the induction of retributive suffering. Furthermore, regarding the summary of the animal realm, it says: "All these are likewise summoned and induced by the karma of one's own false imaginings.

It returns to be received by oneself. As clarified in the sutras, every joint is bound by the delusions that attract [retribution] and the retribution thus attracted;

Because people are unable to synthesize these with a subtle mind, the heart-seal of the Buddhas and Patriarchs remains buried within the secondary principles. This shall be addressed again when reaching the time of the textual commentary.

Now, because this practitioner is within the samādhi of meditative concentration, past habitual tendencies are stirred;

or perhaps celestial māras, evil spirits, or external conditions and adverse circumstances seize the opportunity to manifest alternately, thereby harming the dhyāna-concentration and dragging [the practitioner] into [saṃsāra].
The wheel of suffering is precisely that which gives rise to the capacity to attract retribution; it is this that must be carefully discerned and refuted.
As the sutra concludes after refuting the demon of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-māra*), it says: "Each rests according to their own preferences, their minds deluded by former habits."

When the karma that has produced these experiences is exhausted, one inevitably falls into the Avīci Hell. Each person, through the deluded mind conditioned by what they love and have previously practiced, immediately gives rise—by means of contemplation—to the very mental state that formerly summoned retribution;
thus, they rest of their own accord and remain fixed within the objective realm without progressing.

Or, they may remain within the views of dhyāna, afflicted by karma, even encountering the nine realms and fifty *skandha*-māras of the Two Vehicles. When the karma is finally exhausted, they fall into hell, which is precisely the retribution they summoned.

This is the fruit. Although these two both belong to the secondary branches (*śākhā-pratyaṅga*) and are capable of attracting retribution, they differ because one is a present active habitual cause (*vāsanā-hetu*), while the other is produced through cultivation based on past [seeds].

"Taking what can summon retribution" means to take away; it refers to taking away the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) and the five mental consciousnesses (*pañca-manovijñāna*), as well as their associated feeling, perception, formations, and mind.
These mental factors, being associated with the faculties and objects, will inevitably create karma that invites the suffering of retribution within the seven realms of existence.

Therefore, for now, we shall set these aside and proceed below to examine them through the remaining states of mind. Furthermore, one must identify those that arise as belonging to the afflictions (*kleśa*);
this excludes the other nine objects. If they arise, one observes them; if they do not arise, one does not observe them. If even a single instance arises, it is immediately capable of...
Because harmful contemplations draw forth rebirth, they are designated as "arousing" and "attaining," and thus they are capable of summoning retribution; these are likewise set aside for now.

Only when the ten vehicles of contemplating the aggregates (*skandha*) are complete will one employ the ten vehicles of contemplation to break through them. This principle applies to the remaining aggregates and sense-bases (*āyatana*).

As stated at the end of the "Pervasiveness of Breaking Dharmas" section in the fourth fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*: "Regarding the mind of total ignorance, it may not necessarily be appropriate; one should further proceed through the remaining single minds, or..."
Regarding the mind of desire and the mind of anger—when such minds arise, they are immediately empty, provisional, and the Middle. This is as explained in the general section [of the *Mohe zhiguan*].

Furthermore, it is said that what was previously discussed refers specifically to contemplating the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) in this manner; the same applies to the other four aggregates.

It is likewise for the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Notes) states: "Contemplating the totality of ignorance (*avidyā*) is not necessarily appropriate for everyone; one must open up [the contemplation] according to the individual."
By distinguishing these separately, the two chapters on the general and the specific become clear and evident.

Now, since both types of secondary branches—those arising from active manifestation and those acquired through attainment—have been examined in detail without obstruction, one naturally flows into the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Therefore, we know that within the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the contemplation of the mind of universal ignorance serves as a model for traversing the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the nine objects; this is precisely what the first seven fascicles of the present sutra treat in terms of the general.

The mind of ignorance is cultivated and realized through clarity (*vidyā*). The final three fascicles, concerning the specific karmic retributions that are summoned, and the two major chapters on cultivation and realization, do not differ in the slightest detail.

Question: In the present sutra, the general refutation and manifestation [of reality] must first be fully perfected in terms of understanding, practice, and realization before one investigates the seven destinies.
However, in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, this "refutation" occurs within the fourth of the ten stages of contemplation (*daśa-yāna*) regarding the aggregates (*skandha*). Why is there this difference?

Based on this, one follows understanding to initiate practice, and when practice reaches its ultimate limit, all flows spontaneously into the Dharma-gate.
The sequence from beginning to end must be followed without any interpolation or deviation into other matters.

Next, because Ānanda had a doubt as to how the seven realms of existence arise, [the Buddha] further demonstrated the causes that invite the retributive suffering of these seven realms—namely, the ten habitual causes (*daśa-śīla-hetu*) which are the manifest, secondary branches—and that the retribution thus invited constitutes the seven realms themselves. Master Tiantai contemplated this...

Having already manifested the inconceivable realm through mindfulness, one must necessarily and universally shatter the delusions of the five abodes. Since the universal shattering of all dharmas has been established based on the mind of total ignorance,
there is a concern that practitioners of the latter age might believe that only the observing mind-king can thus universally shatter them,
and fail to realize that the five consciousnesses and the three minds selected below [the mind-king] prior to observation are likewise capable of such universal shattering.

Is it not so? Therefore, one may apply this analogy by saying: throughout the remaining [stages], every state of mind consists of the three truths and the three contemplations; this applies equally to the remaining aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*).
Thus, we know that although the scriptural treatises seem to present these examples in a sequential order—first general and later specific—the underlying meaning remains fundamentally the same.

Question: In the present sutra, the demonic afflictions regarding the aggregates (*skandhamāra*) are only analyzed after the realization of the fruit. Yet, in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, the contemplation of the aggregates occurs as soon as...
If one has completed the practice but the realization has not yet been explained, what are the nine objects of contemplation? The answer is:

The Buddha, being a person who has attained the ultimate fruit, naturally explains in detail the dharma-gates realized within his own mind regarding the stage of fruition. The Great Master, while provisionally abiding in the five grades of practitioners, speaks of the dharma-gates practiced within his own mind;
for him, the ten vehicles alone are sufficient. Therefore, in the *Zhi guan*, it is appropriate to contemplate the ten [objects] within the contemplation of the aggregates (*skandha*).

According to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, one should observe that the attainment [of the fruits] arises immediately after mounting [the vehicle], whereas it is appropriate to identify the five aggregates as demons of attainment only once the realization of the fruit has been completed.

Question: Since the first seven fascicles of this scripture explain cultivation and realization solely in terms of the mind of universal ignorance (*avidyā*), how can it be that the second fascicle contains the destruction of the five aggregates, the six sense bases (*āyatana*), and the twelve bases (*dhātu*), as well as further explanations?
[Question: Is this [the method of] the seven elements and twenty-five perfect penetrations (*yuan-tong*)? [Answer:

This is because, once the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of *śamatha* has been manifested, the principle must be harmonized with all phenomena to achieve the great understanding of the Perfect [Teaching]. It is not a separate contemplation of the sense-fields (*āyatana*) and their secondary branches.

Only when one reaches the fourth stage of "Pervasive Destruction of Phenomena" (*po-fa-pien*) within the practice of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* does one then apply this analogy to all things, desiring to harmonize the objects of perception so that they are universally integrated.

The meaning of this statement is indeed coincidental. The Great Master sought the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* to verify his practice of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, yet he did not realize that *śamatha-vipaśyanā* is entirely identical to the *Śūraṅgama*.
Thus, although the *Śūraṅgama* had not yet been formally categorized by the Great Master’s hand, it is clear that it is indeed the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Nevertheless, how could the Great Master have been unaware of this? He merely feigned ignorance for the sake of instruction.
Thus it was said. Yingzhen remarked: "I came wishing to consult with Mañjuśrī, yet instead I have encountered a minor Śākyamuni of this land.
It is only fitting that the two Buddhas share the same heart and the scriptures and treatises follow the same path. The commentaries of former sages were not lacking in talent and eloquence;

yet, regarding the two chapters on the seven destinies and the five aggregates, they both failed to provide a definitive indication. Since the latter two [chapters] offer no firm grounding, one begins to suspect even the former.

Both [masters] practiced divination by shooting arrows over covered objects; each was correct in their respective methods, yet neither was willing to yield to the other. Consequently, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* has remained an unresolved case of doubt for a thousand years.
Although Master Lingyao, whenever he presided over a lecture, also respectfully followed the previous commentaries to manage the occasion for the time being, he could not set his mind at ease.
This lingering unease never left him throughout his walking, standing, sitting, or reclining. Now, however—
Having fortunately attained the intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs acting with one mind, I dare not harbor private views, but record this for future generations.

It is my hope that by exhausting this "measure of a ladle," I may look up and repay the Buddha’s kindness; how could I presume to claim that my analysis of the minute details and extraction of the scriptures constitute a definitive treatise for resolving doubts?

Regarding the second, the contemplation of the meditative object: this sutra takes the present single thought-moment of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate), the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), as the object of contemplation.
It employs the contemplation of emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle Way as the means of observation.

By contemplating this single thought-moment, one directly manifests the wondrous true suchness-nature (*tathatā-svabhāva*) of the three *tathāgatagarbhas*, continuing until the ultimate perfection of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa. This is because this [nature] is the source of the mind, prior to its delusion.
Before this [awakening], it was only this; after becoming deluded, it was only this; the opening of understanding through names and words was only this;
and the ultimate accomplishment of the fruit was only this. What is meant is that, in delusion, one flows through the three paths; in awakening, there is the supreme function within the fruit.

In principle, these are the inherent qualities of the nature—the conditions and the understanding; in fact, they are the three causes of cultivated virtue. Thus, these four layers are all established based upon the true reality (*dharmatā*) within delusion.
Once sentient beings have become deluded regarding this, there arises a false and illusory state upon their very substance, causing them to undergo the cycle of birth and death in vain.
Now, if they wish to return to the source, they must investigate that original source before they can eliminate their delusions; it is like falling from the ground.

Returning from the ground, one realizes that the reason the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain ultimate fruition and manifest the substance of the Great Buddha-Crown (Uṣṇīṣa) does not exceed the perfection of this single, original thought-moment. How could there be anything further added or anything else separately cultivated?
It is like the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), which suddenly becomes stained with dust until it is as black as lacquer; it is also like this.
It is simply a mirror; there is nothing more than the delusory dust upon its surface. When one wishes to reveal the mirror’s original radiance, this too merely involves polishing the mirror itself;

there is no separate method for revealing light apart from the mirror. Once the process is complete and the dust is cleared so that the light emerges, this merely restores the mirror’s inherent radiance;
there is no addition of anything external to the mirror. It is simply that the delusion has ceased.

It is merely a delusion. Although Yanjadada ran about in a state of confused madness, his original head was never lost. When his madness subsides and he regains his head, how could it have increased at all?
All Tathāgatas, upon first contemplating the aggregates (*skandhas*) and the mind, attained the ultimate fruit.

so that its own unconfused, inherent nature may manifest. Therefore, at the beginning of this assembly at the Śūraṅgama Sūtra,
when Ānanda first requested the method by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain Bodhi, the Buddha immediately—
One should sequentially and carefully inquire into and extract this single thought-moment of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) to serve as the object of contemplation.
As it is said: "To see this nature in this way is the mind, not the eye," and so forth. Indeed, within all the world, nothing exists apart from name (*nāma*) and form (*rūpa*).

If one wishes to contemplate according to reality, one should simply contemplate name and form. If a person recognizes the mind, they will find that throughout the great earth there is not even an inch of soil [that is not mind]. How much more so...
The Buddha-dharma is too sublime and sentient beings are too numerous, making it difficult for those with a beginner's mind. If one contemplates the mind, however, it is both proximate and essential.

Therefore, this sutra reveals to practitioners that the fundamental *ālaya-vijñāna* (the "mind of the aggregates")—proximate and essential—is the object of contemplation, thereby manifesting the essence of the Great Uṣṇīṣa, the Three Tathāgata-garbhas.
One must know that the essence of the Great Uṣṇīṣa is never separate from the mind.
It exists. It is simply that we have fully realized the fundamental mind of our own present single thought-moment.
For when this mind has not yet given rise to a single thought, the three thousand [dharmas] lie in profound latency as the "principle-endowment" (*li-jù*);

once a single thought has moved, the three thousand arise simultaneously as the "phenomenal-creation" (*shi-zào*). However, at the time of phenomenal creation, there are two different conditions: the defiled and the pure. Regarding the pure...
The dependent origination of the three thousand [dharmas] is both in essence and in function eternally co-existent.
When the dependent origination of the three thousand is in a state of defilement, it is collectively termed ignorance (*avidyā*) within delusion. Ignorance means "lack of clarity";

it is a false fabrication upon the essence itself, like dust and grime on a mirror—it is not originally present, but arises falsely through delusion. Because the Buddha teaches sentient beings to investigate and shatter this falsehood, he employs the seven... [factors].
By pursuing and tracking this single point of spirit, the false root of life finds no place to hide.
Once the culprit has been exposed, one must directly deliver a shout to sever its accumulated delusions—what is called "dealing a single blow beneath the root of life.
When this delusion is removed, the light of the Great Perfect Mirror manifests spontaneously from within; it is not obtained from without, for it originally relies upon the fundamental mind.

Thus it is made manifest. Therefore, to observe the single thought-moment of the present and thereby reveal the inconceivable realm is the most direct and the most perfect, sudden Dharma—that which is simultaneously delusion and reality. People of the world do not understand this;

instead, they claim that the entire substance of the conscious mind in the present thought-moment is delusion and cannot be relied upon to reveal the Real. How could they know that the essence of this mind is entirely Real?

Moreover, after many rounds of critical examination and refutation, the conceptualization of a self-nature is found to be entirely empty, and the fundamental clarity reveals itself spontaneously. This corresponds to the "Selection of Objects" (*viṣaya-vibhāga*) in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* and *Mohe Zhiguan*:
when all deluded states of active manifestation lose their basis, only this single thought-moment of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) manifests before one.

To speak of "one thought-moment" is already to have emptied a thousand or ten thousand thoughts; it is what is meant by the saying, "Once you grasp the One, all affairs are finished. To raise the mind—
The King has already departed; it is this master—the sovereign lord—who manifests and activates all the various minds that serve as his messengers.
To speak of "manifesting before one" means that one is no longer shrouded by the obscurations of deluded karma, but rather solitary clarity is revealed alone.
Is this point where solitary clarity is revealed alone not the very manifestation of *śamatha*? It is precisely this single thought-moment that is the three thousand [realms].
The three thousand worlds are precisely one thought-moment. This one thought-moment does not exist prior to the three thousand, nor do the three thousand exist subsequent to it.

They are neither identical nor different, yet the wondrous provisional nature is manifest, with all phenomena appearing in their full array. They are neither empty nor existent; thus, *dhyāna* is sovereign and the Middle Way is perfectly luminous.
It is like a mirror from which dust has been removed: its radiance appears spontaneously, neither coming from without nor emerging from within—an inconceivable reality.
Since the objective realm is manifested as the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), is this not indeed clear and evident?
Yet, does the Buddha merely command sentient beings in this sutra to contemplate and investigate the present mental aggregates? It is so in every sutra; it is likewise in every treatise.

The Buddha commands the bhikṣus to practice the Path by contemplating the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Bodhisattvas contemplate consciousness, sensation, perception, formations, and form, up to all modes of being (*sarvākāra*).
Regarding "Wisdom," the *Awakening of Faith* states: "There is a dharma capable of giving rise to the root of faith in the Mahāyāna.
This so-called dharma is the mind of all sentient beings. Furthermore, the wondrous Dharma is the mind. The essence of this wondrous mind is complete, like a wish-fulfilling jewel;
thus, the Dharma-realm of the *Avataṃsaka*, the True Aspect of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the secret treasury of the *Nirvāṇa*, and the wisdom of the *Prajñāpāramitā* are all identical to it."
The mind is that which is discussed. If one claims that there are dharmas external to the mind, it is as if claiming there are dharmas external to the true mark (*dharmatā*). The Patriarch said:

"The aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*)—these three all serve as objects. This is because for a practitioner who has received a body, who does not have the burden of the aggregates and sense bases manifest before them?
If contemplating the mind is both proximate and essential, then the consciousness of the mind is precisely the locus from which contemplation arises.
This is the gateway for entering into principle. It is truly because the mind can be all Buddhas, the mind can be all sentient beings, the mind can be heaven, and the mind can be hell.

The mind is itself the Buddhas; the mind is itself sentient beings. Furthermore, it is because the Buddhas are identical to the mind, sentient beings are identical to the mind, heaven is identical to the mind, and hell is identical to the mind.
While there is delusion and enlightenment in the case of sentient beings and Buddhas, herein there is neither delusion nor enlightenment. Sentient...

The Buddha has concealment and manifestation, whereas this [mind] has neither concealment nor manifestation. Buddhas and sentient beings exist across the three periods of time, whereas this alone is eternally abiding.
An ancient said: "It is simply a matter of being without mind; as soon as there is even a slight stirring of mind, the three thousand worlds are fully present.
Therefore, all sentient beings rely entirely upon this mind to emerge from birth and death within the vast and boundless great waves and realize Bodhi. The Buddhas of the ten directions likewise...
By bringing this mind to ultimate fulfillment, one gives rise to great compassion within the five turbidities of the triple world, turning the wheel of Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
If one were to sweep it all away and discard it, one would sever the very foundation for sentient beings to achieve Buddhahood and destroy the basis upon which all Buddhas attain the Way.
Moreover, this sutra specifically emphasizes the mind as the means to clarify what was obscured and to integrate the mind so as to realize the secret treasury.
To insist that [the teachings of] Tiantai are "not used" is perhaps even to surpass the words of the Buddhas. Jiaoguang says, "The six consciousnesses of Tiantai are not used.
Little does he realize that these consciousnesses are the fundamental basis shared by all Buddhas and sentient beings;
how could they be relegated solely to the Tiantai school? It is like the sun and moon in the sky, which all who have eyes can see—yet the blind cannot.
If people do not see it, one might say that the sky has no sun; yet is it reasonable to claim that all the people in the world likewise cannot see the sun?

Nevertheless, the statement that "the eyes' light intermingles and the faculty [root] functions, but consciousness does not" also has its basis in scripture; it is merely that [the commentator] has misunderstood it.
He saw that after the sevenfold refutation of the self-nature in the sutra, Ānanda still identified the one who investigates, pursues, and seeks as being the self.
[The student] takes this to be the mind. However, the Tathāgata directly lets out a shout and says, "This is not your mind.
Based on this, Jiaoguang immediately asserts that since the "consciousness-mind" has already been personally refuted by the Tathāgata’s own mouth, it should not be employed.

What he fails to realize is that what the Tathāgata refuted was the攀緣 (pān'yuán) — the grasping after and chasing after objects — which is a false fabrication upon the essence; it was not a refutation of the consciousness-essence itself, the true master. This...
If even the slightest trace of subtle falsehood remains, the mind will be clouded, disturbed, and chaotic, and its principle will be entirely lost.

Once the Buddha has shattered this through his shout, the mirror becomes pure and bright, and the substance of the mind suddenly manifests—this is what is meant by the so-called "nature-consciousness’s clear knowing," the "awakened clarity of true consciousness," which is "pure and fundamental, pervading the entire dharma-realm. How could this be like merely rubbing away the dust and grime from a mirror?

It is not that the luminosity of the mirror-substance has been discarded; it is simply that when it is defiled by the delusions of dust before it, it undergoes transformation according to conditions (*anuvartana-pratyaya*).

When True Suchness is in a state of delusion, that delusion is termed the six consciousnesses. Now, when delusion is removed and the substance is revealed, it remains unchanged while following conditions, pervading the entire Dharma-realm—this is precisely the clear knowing of the nature-consciousness (*prakṛti-vijñāna*). How could there ever have been two? It is also like a soiled garment within...
The "ornamentation of the body's necklaces" refers solely to the elder; it does not mean that apart from the inner body—which is free from defilement—there exists a separate dharma-body of necklaces.
Therefore, one should know that the statement "this is not your mind" is precisely intended to shatter the defiled delusions upon the substance [of the mind] itself.

Jiaoguang misunderstood this, asserting that it must shatter the substance of consciousness so as to render it useless. Furthermore, because the fifth fascicle states that "the nature of consciousness is empty,"...
The phrase "delusion is like flowers in the sky" refers only to the refutation of the six consciousnesses;

it does not yet indicate that this section universally refutes the falsity of the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus). When it says, "To establish knowing-seeing upon knowing-seeing is the root of ignorance;

when knowing-seeing is without seeing, this is nirvana, the untainted and truly pure," is this not to say that once the falsity within the essence of knowing-seeing is absent, then knowing-seeing itself [is revealed]?

Is its essence not the nature of the *nirvāṇagarbha*? Tiantai’s contemplation of the six consciousnesses to reveal the inconceivable realm was established in profound accordance with the Buddha’s intent;
it is certainly not a claim made without basis. Even the use of the term "roots" (*indriya*) is based on the scriptural texts regarding the commencement of cultivation.
When the Buddha revealed the twenty-five perfect penetrations (*āyatana*), he specifically selected the ear-faculty as the entry point for the Path.

Consequently, they have come to hold a biased attachment, using this scripture exclusively for the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*). How could they know that the mention of the "faculty of hearing" is merely a skillful means (*upāya*) for entering the gate?
Indeed, when a practitioner initiates cultivation, any of the twenty-five gates may serve as a skillful means for entering the Way.

Now, because the faculty of hearing is the sharpest among the sentient beings of this Sahā world, it is most suitable for them to enter through hearing and develop contemplation within the mind; therefore, [the Buddha] specifically...
Select this. You should know that at the moment the contemplation is perfected and the principle is revealed, one has already forgotten the external, auditory expedient.
How could one whose practice from beginning to end remains stuck in the expedient ever achieve the perfect completion of mental contemplation?

Expedients are like the wooden wedge used for knocking on a door or the raft used for crossing a river. If you remain attached to the faculty of hearing and fail to enter the mind to achieve completion, [you will not succeed].
If one contemplates [in this way], these very ear-faculties will instead become obstacles.
Becoming entangled and attached, they serve as the root of birth and death, dragging one into the cycle of saṃsāra without leisure. As the Sūtra says: "Sentient beings are attached everywhere.
The Buddha taught the expedient means for entering the gate, yet worldly people take these expedients for reality and cannot enter the True; how deeply pitiable they are! It is just like this:
The Great Being Avalokiteśvara, in the presence of the ancient Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, first entered the stream from within hearing and forgot the objects of hearing.
Once that entry was exhausted, the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly ceased to arise; thus, both the faculty of the ear and the sounds as its objects vanished together.
Thereafter, he attained such an exhaustion of hearing that even what is heard was exhausted, and the nature of hearing itself became empty. This nature of hearing—
Only when [the object] is absent can one realize that the perceiver is empty, and thus the contemplation of emptiness manifests before one.
I have never heard it said that by dwelling in attachment to the ear-faculty, to form-and-matter, or to顽空 (stubborn emptiness), one can achieve the most perfect realization of emptiness.

One should know that if even the contemplation of emptiness is difficult to accomplish while dwelling in attachment to the ear-faculty, how much more so is the wondrous contemplation of the Perfect Middle when cessation and quiescence manifest?
One must understand that the ear is a material substance of stubborn emptiness; it is entirely a faculty of insentient birth-and-death.

How can one rely upon it to open understanding or initiate practice? Not only is it impossible to rely upon it for the profound cultivation of wondrous contemplation, but even the shallow act of hearing sounds is not something obtained by the ear-faculty itself.
It must necessarily depend on the internal sovereign of the conscious mind to respond to external objects.
Only when the dust is settled can one hear. A sutra says: "To see this nature in this way is the mind, not the eye. An ancient said:
"When the mind is not present, one looks but does not see; hears but does not hear; eats but does not know the flavor. Is this not so?
If it were said that cultivation belongs to the nature of hearing, then the nature of hearing would be identical to consciousness, differing only in being the branch and the root;
thus, when Avalokiteśvara’s mental contemplation was slightly perfected, he spoke of the exhaustion of both "hearing" and "that which is heard," thereby discarding even this nature of hearing itself.

From this, we know that the specific basis for the secret cause of cultivation and realization in this sutra is the *ālaya*-consciousness (*yin-xin*), which serves as the object of contemplation to reveal the Great Buddha-Crown.

As for the essence: if it is merely a temporary reliance on hearing as a provisional means for first entering the gate, then the Sūtra says, "The principle of returning to the source is non-dual, yet the provisional means have many gates.
Are the twenty-five sages not many? Is entry through the gate of the ear not itself a provisional means?
If one were to cling to this passage and maintain that entering by means of the faculty of the ear constitutes the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty, [that would be a mistake].

Which sūtra does not enter through the faculty of hearing? Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana attained realization through the conditions of hearing; this too is the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing.
Kāśyapa and Aññā-Koṇḍañña attained the Way upon hearing the Four Noble Truths and the "Come hither" call; these too are the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing.

Throughout the fifty years of the Buddha’s teaching—encompassing the *Avataṃsaka*, *Mṛgadāva*, *Vaipulya*, *Prajñāpāramitā*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and *Mahāparinirvāṇa* sūtras—all who realized awakening did so by means of the faculty of hearing.
All the disciples received the Buddha’s oral teachings and entered [the Way]; all of them attained the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing.

Xiangyan striking the bamboo, Baizhang’s single shout, and Huineng at Caoxi hearing the response to "do not dwell on anything, but let the mind arise"—all these were instances of the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing.

These are all merely expedient means for attaining perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*). One must understand that the Buddha, in accordance with the circumstances of this Sahā world, generally causes beings to enter through the expedient of the auditory faculty (*śrotra-indriya*).
How could one misinterpret the Buddha’s intent and dogmatically cling to an expedient as the true object of contemplation in this sutra?
As the sutra says: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions have each practiced cultivation within every one of the eighteen realms."
They attain perfect, unsurpassed Bodhi, and during that interval there is no distinction of superior or inferior.
However, because you are of inferior capacity and have not yet attained sovereign wisdom therein, I proclaim that one should enter deeply through a single gate.
Once entered, there is no delusion, and those six faculties of cognition are simultaneously purified. Furthermore, the Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "These twenty-five who are beyond training..."
Each of the Bodhisattvas spoke of their initial expedient means for attaining the Way, all saying that through cultivation they had attained perfect penetration.

In their actual practice, there was truly no distinction of superiority or inferiority, nor of priority or sequence. I now wish to cause Ānanda to awaken to which of the twenty-five practices is suited to his faculties;
furthermore, after my parinirvāṇa, for the sake of the sentient beings of this world who enter the Bodhisattva Vehicle seeking the [Unsurpassed Way].
Regarding the superior path, by what gate of skillful means can it be easily accomplished? Based on this explicit text, it is clear that this refers to the skillful means for entering the gate;
how could it ever be pointed to as the ultimate reality? Furthermore, when Mañjuśrī received his command to select [the teachings], he also said:
"The nature of returning to the source is non-dual, yet there are many gates of skillful means. The sacred nature is all-pervasive; whether following or opposing, all are skillful means."

Furthermore, it says: "Truly, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, questioned me regarding various skillful means (*upāya*), there is no doubt that within this gate, the skillful means are easily accomplished.
While it is stated everywhere that these are skillful means, when has the ear-faculty ever been pointed out as the ultimate?

It is simply that in all sutras, the skillful means enter through the ear, yet this is not explicitly stated. If one were to clearly point to and select [this method] exclusively, it is found only in this present sutra."
Thus, one knows that the statement "employing the faculties but not the consciousness" is truly a case of abandoning the root to pursue the branches. Furthermore, I ask:
what is the basis for the faculty of the ear being able to hear, and from where does it come? Now, the essence of the single, bright, and pure spirit divides to form the six harmonious combinations.
When it resides in the ear, it is called hearing; when in the eye, it is called seeing; and so on, up to when it resides in the body, it is called touching.

Thus we know that the fundamental single mind-consciousness is like a monkey that reflects everywhere through six windows; therefore, there arise the functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
If there were no internal "host" or master, then how could the external eyes, ears, and the six sense-faculties—being mere material forms within a void—be capable of hearing or seeing?
As the Sūtra says: "In this way, the nature of seeing is the mind, not the eye. This can be stated as follows:
The nature of hearing is the mind, not the eye. The Sūtra says: "If you were inside a room, would the door be able to see? If that were so, why would those who are already dead have no sight?
Let me illustrate this by analogy: if you were inside a room, would the door be able to hear? If that were so, why would those who are already dead have no hearing?
The faculty of hearing depends upon the provisional consciousness-mind and its fundamental basis; why then do you [assert it] one-sidedly?
To calculate the roots of form and emptiness as the ultimate dharma for entering the Way— is this not an extreme case of abandoning the root to pursue the branches?

○ To say that "emptiness, the provisional, and the middle" constitute the subject that performs the contemplation refers to the very first method by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attained the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* of Bodhi, as requested by Ānanda at the beginning of this sutra.
It is well. Thus, the Tathāgata first employs the seven rounds of provisional inquiry to refute his false conceptualizations.
Next, he cuts through the traces of habitual tendencies with a single shout of the True Truth.

Thereafter, he gradually guides and leads him to reveal and manifest *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, whereby the contemplation of entering emptiness from the provisional is perfected. Yet you still do not understand that all things are floating...
The various illusory manifestations of the sensory dusts arise in their very place and perish in that same place; their nature is truly the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Thus it is even so for the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense bases (*āyatana*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
These emerge from emptiness and provisionally assemble all phenomena; they are all fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, wherein the entire cosmos is fully manifested, and this is samādhi.

Once the contemplation of the objects is accomplished, one then fuses the seven elements—both matter and mind—such that they are all "true emptiness within the nature of form" and "true form within the nature of emptiness," pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
These two contemplations serve as the skillful means for entering the contemplation of the Middle Way, the Supreme Meaning, which is the response to the request for *dhyāna*.
If one follows the sequence of breaking down and reconciling [the delusions], it proceeds first through *śamatha* and then through *samādhi*.
In terms of theoretical exposition, this is identical to the three successive contemplations (*tri-vipaśyanā*) of the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Necklace Sūtra).

If one relies on the perfect synthesis—wherein the three Tathāgatagarbhas transcend both identity and difference, and both being and non-being, such that they are neither identical nor non-identical—this corresponds to the "one mind and three contemplations" of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Generally, when revealing the methods for practitioners to cultivate the Dharma, words cannot be manifested all at once and matters cannot be undertaken impulsively; thus, a sequential approach is necessary. This reaches the point where delusion is eliminated and truth is exhausted, so that the principles are fully realized.

The Dharma of single penetration must necessarily be perfectly integrated (*yuanrong*). Furthermore, if it were not sequential, delusions would not be exhausted; if it were not perfectly integrated, sublime understanding would not be complete.
Moreover, as the sutra precedes the Vaipulya (*fangdeng*) teachings, the intent of its classification—first the distinct and later the perfect—is all the more clear.
Thus, although Ānanda requested the perfect threefold contemplation of sublime *śamatha*, when the Tathāgata proceeded to reveal it for him, Ānanda...
I could not help but demonstrate the middle and lower stages merely as a sequential process of understanding.

Only after asking again in sequence until the internal realization of the disciple was opened did I universally integrate all things to establish them as the identical Treasury of Nature (*dharmadhātu*), thereby repaying Ānanda’s initial request for the three contemplations to be entirely wondrous.
Furthermore, the method of the three contemplations in this sutra is that by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions achieve [enlightenment].
This is the correct path to Bodhi. It is the essential secret for sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu* to transcend birth and death. Ordinary people bound by fetters possess turbulent delusions;

they must rely upon the wisdom of emptiness to wash away the dust of their emotions. Like the precious sword of the Vajra King, one must directly sever the life-root so that not even a single thread remains obstructed.
Only then can the dust be purified, the light arise, and the original reality be revealed in its solitude. Upon reaching this state:
When the opposition has ceased and all delusions have vanished, and not a single thought arises, names and forms are entirely extinguished;
