fundamentally, there is no such thing as the "name" of empty contemplation (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). It is simply that sentient beings have hitherto been bound by their deluded minds to the myriad phenomena;

they rely on this wondrous wisdom to directly empty all conditioned existence right before them, which is merely a provisional name for "empty contemplation. How could there truly be a "contemplation of emptiness" existing within the breast?

Alas! If one merely retains the name of "contemplation of emptiness" within this context, then the cycle of birth and death will remain vast and long-lasting. How, then, could one transcend birth and death?

It is just like the "impermanence" taught by the Tripitaka masters: beginning from the *kalā* (the smallest unit of time) and culminating in the full manifestation [of destruction], such that even Mount Sumeru and the great earth are utterly consumed and swept away by the kalpa-fire until nothing remains. How much more so for the true emptiness of *śamatha*?

How powerful [is this ignorance]! That worldly people cling to the expedient means of the ear-faculty as being the true reality is simply because they have never even touched upon the "small emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).
How much more so for those above them; although the various devas of the higher realms possess profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), they lack this wisdom of emptiness.

Consequently, they are only able to suppress and sever the afflictions of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), yet they cannot destroy their various views (*dṛṣṭi*) and remain entirely within saṃsāra. This is comparable to those who uphold the precepts...
The Master Qiu restrained his body and speech as if holding an oil bowl; how arduous and difficult this was! This was also because he lacked this wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*);

he could only temporarily suspend the retribution of karma, yet since afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) remained entirely intact, how could he have avoided the cycle of birth and death? Thus, we know that this single wisdom of emptiness is [of paramount importance].
This is the very root for the practitioners of the four teachings and for all Buddhas of the three periods appearing in the world to attain enlightenment.
Therefore, this present sutra places sole emphasis on the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. Nevertheless, the only fear is that the deluded mind is not empty.

Once the mind is empty, then spontaneously every dharma is manifest and realized, and every phenomenon accords with the Way; the myriad phenomena are fully present—this is called the *samādhi* of the provisional contemplation of names.

Neither being nor non-being is the Middle Way of *dhyāna*. Just as images naturally appear when the grime on a mirror has been removed, the identity and differencelessness of the mirror, its luminosity, and the images constitute the threefold contemplation in perfect fusion (*yuanrong*).
In reality, however, this is simply the contemplation of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) to reveal the primordially existing single mind.
Even upon this fundamental mind, there are no provisional names for the three contemplations. Thus do the Buddhas of the ten directions...
The Buddha, by means of this wondrous wisdom, shattered all delusions to reveal the ultimate fundamental mind.

Therefore, he sequentially pointed to the path he himself had traversed to clearly demonstrate it for those to come, so that sentient beings might rely upon it to advance swiftly and first ascend to the shore of the Way;
hence, there is the designation of the "Three Contemplations. Jiaoguang, not realizing that this wondrous [wisdom] is the core, claims instead that the Three Contemplations belong to...
The Tiantai [teachings] cannot be disregarded or set aside. Now, as one traverses the Great Way, both the noble and the humble follow its course.

If sentient beings settle their minds within the burning house, they will naturally find that there is no need to rely on other paths. If one truly wishes to compete in escaping the wheel of suffering, how could there be anyone who abandons this and seeks another way?
As it is said, "One must exit through a door; which door would one not pass through? If you claim these teachings cannot be relied upon or employed, [you are mistaken].

This has blocked the true path of the sublime śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna—the means by which sentient beings within the Dharma-realm emerge from birth-and-death and achieve Bodhi—causing them instead to enter the deviant paths of constructing birth-and-death and falling into the three miserable realms. How tragic!
Furthermore, regarding this correct path of the three contemplations, Ānanda did not know it and thus requested it of the Tathāgata; because he requested it, the Tathāgata revealed it.

One must first have *śamatha*, next *samādhi*, and finally *dhyāna*. Since these answers to the questions are clear and explicit in every chapter, how can they be attributed solely to the Tiantai school?
Tiantai merely established these terms based on the sutras for the sake of the Bodhisattva Dharmadāna.
Furthermore, this dharma-gate of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) is not taught exclusively in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*; the *Ratnaketu-parivarta* (Yingluo jing) also speaks of the three.

Contemplation. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* elucidates the three contemplations; the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Ārya-bodhimaṇḍala-vairocana-abhisambodhi*) speaks of the three contemplations; the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also teaches the three contemplations; and the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* explains the three contemplations.

If one were to categorize and penetrate these through the lens of the three contemplations, then the nature of the path, consciousness, prajñā, bodhi, the Mahāyāna body, and the virtues of the Three Jewels—nirvāṇa included—each consist of these three dharmas.
This applies to everything discussed during the fifty years [of the Buddha’s teaching] regarding the Tathāgata’s attainment of bodhi.

For sentient beings to emerge from birth-and-death and proceed from delusion to enlightenment, there is no essential method for progressing from the shallow to the profound that lies outside the sublime wisdom of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).
How could it be that this cannot be relied upon and applied? How could one then attribute its origin solely to Tiantai?

If, in fact, the three contemplations were not to be relied upon, it would not only sever the correct path by which the beings of the *dharmadhātu* emerge from birth-and-death, but would also disparage the Tathāgata.

"The teachings of a single lifetime are all erroneous discourse. Even the path by which the Tathāgata himself reached the place of the Human Treasure through the three contemplations would be mistaken.
Furthermore, even the Bodhi attained by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions through this śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna might not have been achieved [according to your view].
(Lingyao) Fortunately, having encountered the Buddha-vehicle, I am able to set it forth."

I have looked up to and admired [the teachings]. Although my own understanding is dim and limited, my intent is to benefit others. Fearing that those who come after might not know [this] and would thus slander the Dharma and fall into suffering, I have briefly provided this clarification.
This is not a matter of stubbornly clinging to partiality or arbitrarily asserting what is right or wrong; were there any such bias, the devas and nāgas would surely reprove me.
The explanation of the title is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the title of the sutra; second, the explanation of the translator.

Within the title of the sutra, there is first the explanation of the main title, followed by the explanation of its specific name. Generally, titles are analyzed according to five layers; here, four levels of explanation are provided. First, the presentation of the headings.
Second, the explanation; third, the citation of evidence; fourth, the arising [of the treatise].
First, regarding the heading: this sutra takes "person and dharma" as its title, and the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha as its essence.

The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* is its primary principle (*mūla*), and severing craving while distancing oneself from worldly dust is its function (*prayojana*). Its teaching aspect (*śāstralakṣaṇa*) is that it is revealed through the Vaipulya [sūtras] to become the *amṛta* (the "cream of the cream").

Regarding the two types of explanation: first, the explanation of the title. This sūtra is titled according to both persons and dharmas; the titles have both general and specific aspects. "Mahābuddha... [and so forth].
"Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata Guhyahetu Xiuzheng Liao yi Zhu Pusa Wanxing Shou Lengyan" consists of nineteen characters that constitute the specific title (*viśeṣa-nāman*).
"Sūtra" is the general title (*sāmānya-nāman*). Now, I shall first explain the specific title. As stated therein:

"Among the specific titles there are three phrases. First, the three characters 'Da Foding' (Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa) form one phrase. Second, from 'Rulai' (Tathāgata) downwards constitutes the second..."
There are two phrases. Next, the section beginning with "Then all the bodhisattvas" constitutes the third phrase. Following this, the conclusion of the sutra contains five titles;
however, since only three are retained in the present primary title while two are omitted, it consists of only nineteen characters.

Regarding the first three characters, Tōshū cites the interpretation of Ōsō, identifying them as the name of a secret mantra (*dhāraṇī*); this explanation is most excellent. Nevertheless, upon examining the meaning within the sutra, it is not limited to a single approach.
It is called the "Buddha-Usnīṣa Radiance Mahāsitātapatra Unsurpassed Divine Mantra.
This is the heart-mantra spoken by the Tathāgata from his crown—wherein he manifests as the Unconditioned Mind-Buddha seated upon a precious lotus flower—within the mark of the invisible crown.
Furthermore, it is also said that this mantra is named the "Tathāgata’s Crown. Is it not from this secret mantra that it derives its name? [End of] Chapter One.

The scripture states: "There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which fully embodies the myriad practices and is the wondrously adorned path through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend by a single gate.
Thus, it is beyond doubt that the term "Great Buddha-Crown" (Dàfódǐng) is derived from the teachings of Manifestation (xiǎnjiào).
"Great" (Dà) is a praise for its essential nature; "Buddha-Crown" (Fódǐng) is a designation for supreme reverence. Indeed...
Because the essence of awakening is wondrously luminous and devoid of perceivable characteristics, it pervades all places and transcends all forms of existence.
It is called the Great Uṣṇīṣa because it cannot be fathomed by the four eyes or the two types of wisdom. When explained openly, it is a sūtra;
when explained cryptically, it is a mantra. How could there be two? What is meant by "cryptic" is not the secrecy of the Dharma-wheel of secrets; it refers simply to the Sanskrit language.
Because it had not yet been translated and the people of the Qin state did not understand it, it was called "Mimi" (Secret).

This sutra relates how Ānanda, having entered a brothel and encountered defilement, was clear in his mind yet lacked the power of self-mastery; in terms of its meaning, this constitutes attachment to signs (*nimitta*).
How could this mantra of the Wondrously Bright, Signless, and Most Honorable One fail to bring about liberation? Within the sutra, this mantra is named the "Crown of the Tathāgata."
This spell is indeed named the "Wondrously Bright, Formless, and Transcendent Dharma.
That it is spoken by the transformation Buddha emerging from the light on the crown of the head is because the Way is difficult to know, and thus the Sage must manifest it through symbols.

Therefore, from the crown of Śākyamuni, the Buddha of the Unconditioned Mind appears to speak this Supreme Mind-Spell. From the perspective of that which manifests it, the word "Buddha" may be pointed to [as its referent].

The "Śākyamuni" refers to the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The character "Crown" (*mūrdhan*) may include the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Śākyamuni; however, the "Crown" here specifically denotes the mark of the invisible crown (*anavalokitamūrdhatā*), which directly manifests the dharma body (*dharmakāya*).
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "As soon as he was born, they quickly held him up; though they gazed intently, they could not see his crown. This precisely points to this very mark.
The *Xiyu ji* states: In the past, a Brahmin took a bamboo staff one zhang and six chi long, intending to measure the Buddha’s body.

As soon as it reached one zhang and six chi, it grew another zhang and six chi. When his measuring could not proceed further, he stuck the staff in the ground and departed; the staff subsequently grew into a grove.
Later, a vihāra was established there and named Yaṣṭivana (Staff Forest). Furthermore, the *Vajrapāṇi-guhyaka-sūtra* states:
After the Buddha attained enlightenment, he traveled to Vārāṇasī. Far to the east of this place, there is a buddha named Saṃcintya-puṣpa; his world is named Parigrahavineya.
There is a bodhisattva named Ādhāra who came to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet. Having circumambulated him a thousand times, he thought that he wished to—

He measured the Buddha’s body; immediately, he transformed his own form to be three million three hundred thousand *li* tall, yet he still saw the Buddha’s body to be five hundred forty-three million *zhao-hai* (10^24) and two hundred million *li* tall.

By the Buddha’s supernatural power, he was able to carry it upward to a world in the zenith named Padmavyūha, a hundred billion worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges away, where the Buddha was named Padma. He ascended until he reached that world.
One never beholds the crown of the Śākya-Buddha’s head, nor can one know the distance of the Buddha’s body. When [Śāriputra] went to inquire of that Buddha, he replied:
"Even after the passing of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one still cannot see the crown of the Śākya-Buddha’s head;
the same applies to his wisdom, speech, and radiance. Based on the above scriptural passage, it is clear that the mark of the invisible crown (anavalokitamūrdhatā) constitutes the Dharmakāya.
Since the manifested Buddhas appearing from this crown must arise as retribution (*vipāka*) from the Dharma-body, the Sūtra says:

"At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from his crown a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness. From within the light, thousand-petaled jeweled lotuses emerged, upon which transformed Buddhas sat in the full-lotus posture.
As stated in the Sūtra, are the Buddhas upon the flower pedestals not indeed the retribution-body? The retribution-body is entirely...
Because it is through wisdom alone that one can manifest the path of the signless Dharma-body, the mantra is specifically addressed to Mañjuśrī.
This indicates that although the three bodies are shown therein, the primary focus is the signless Dharma-body; this is the intended meaning of the "image" (xiàng).

From this point, the mantra is proclaimed from the crown of the head to correctly demonstrate the supreme and wondrously luminous principle of the mantra’s signlessness—what further doubt could there be?
Indeed. This expresses the principle elucidated by the divine mantra, and it also expresses the principle elucidated by the scriptural text.
Although the Exoteric and Esoteric differ, their essence is non-dual. Wuxing said: "The title of the scripture is not a metaphor but the Dharma; does it not also pertain to the person?
The Three Bodies are the person, and the fundamental principle is the Dharma. Question: Why is it not called the Buddha-body?

Regarding the term "Buddha’s Crown" (*buddhōṣṇīṣa*), the answer is as follows: If one says that the Buddha-body universally encompasses both emptiness and existence, the present discussion of the Buddha’s crown refers specifically to the Middle Way, the dharma of signlessness.

The *Śūchí* (Explanatory Notes) states: "Emptiness and the provisional are identical to the Middle; the Middle is the essence of the sūtra. The Middle is identical to emptiness and the provisional, yet it also points back to the Middle.
The three truths are all without exception pervasive throughout all places. Based on this passage from the *Śūchí*, the three truths are all pervasive within the sūtra.
The essence is simply the Middle Way. Now, we take only the signless as the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa; yet, what could possibly not be the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa?
The meaning of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa is vast, wondrous, and inexhaustible. What has been explained above is merely the briefest of the brief.

Next, the eight characters "The Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, Realization, and Definitive Meaning" constitute a single phrase. "Tathāgata" refers to the person who has realized the fruit. [End of] Text.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Because one comes by means of the path of reality (*yathābhūta-mārga*) to achieve perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one is called a Tathāgata.

The commentary on this passage explains: "The 'vehicle' (*yāna*) is the wisdom of the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatājñāna*); 'reality' (*tattva*) is the object that is the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatālambana*); the 'path' (*mārga*) is the cause; and 'enlightenment' (*bodhi*) is the fruit.

Based on this, it is known that the single character "such" (*ru*, *tathā*) should be explained in terms of both object and wisdom—that is, the object is such as wisdom, and wisdom is such as the object.
This refers to the objective realm (*viṣaya*). The single character "coming" (*lai*) should be explained in terms of cause and effect.

That is to say, by riding upon the path of reality within the causal stage, one comes to realize the fruit of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Regarding the "esoteric cause" (*mimi-yin*): "esoteric" (*mi*) means secret. As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, Chapter on Lamentation, states:
What is called the "Secret Treasury"? It is like the three dots of the letter *i*: if they are placed side by side, they do not form the letter *i*;
if they are placed vertically, they likewise do not form it. Only when they are like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara does one obtain the letter *i*.
If the three dots are separate, they also cannot form it. I am also like this: the dharma of liberation is not itself Nirvana, yet it is not apart from the Tathāgata.
The body is not nirvāṇa; the Mahāprajñāpāramitā is not nirvāṇa; nor is it nirvāṇa for these three dharmas to be distinct from one another.
Because I now abide in these three dharmas for the sake of sentient beings, it is called "entering nirvāṇa," like the world-character (卍).
What is taught in the Great Sūtra is the fruit of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury of the three virtues; yet the fruit must necessarily correspond to its cause.
The cause of the fruit is called the "esoteric cause" (guhyahetu). What is it? It is said that suffering is the Dharmakāya, afflictions are Prajñā, and karma is Vimukti.
To understand and know them in this way is what is termed the esoteric cause. A sutra says:

"The five aggregates, the six sense bases, and from the twelve bases up to the eighteen elements arise through the combination of causes and conditions; they are falsely produced. When causes and conditions disperse..."

What is called "extinction" is merely a false fabrication. It is utterly impossible to know that arising and ceasing, going and coming, are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha—the eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, and all-pervading nature of wondrous True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Within this true and eternal nature, one seeks in vain for going and coming, delusion and awakening, or birth and death;
nothing at all can be found. Is this not profoundly subtle, as stated in the Sūtra? Question: Why does it not point directly to the wondrous *śamatha*?
"Is samādhi-dhyāna the secret cause? Answer: "This wondrous triple cessation already encompasses cultivation; one should first take understanding and realization as the cause.
Since beginningless time, sentient beings have possessed only afflictions, karma, and suffering, yet their very substance is the three virtues—this meaning is most profound.
One who can understand this understands the triple cessation. Why? Because it transcends thought and deliberation."

Therefore, because it is free from both sense organs and objects, the understanding of the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) is now specifically designated as the "esoteric cause. Cultivating this esoteric cause is called "cultivation according to the definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*).

This is just as the *Ārya-Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* distinguished the various modes of penetration (*vibhūti-prativedha*) and determined that the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) is the most appropriate for the spiritual capacities of those in this land.

Realization based upon this is called realization of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). This is as stated in the *Fifty-five Stages of the True Path to Bodhi*. "Definitive meaning" refers to the ultimate expression of the meaning.
For example, while emptiness and the provisional are not definitive, the Middle Way is definitive; while the separated [teachings] are not definitive, the perfect Middle Way is definitive.
Now, this sutra contains both the provisional and the real; it brings the provisional back to the real, and everything therein is of definitive meaning. This is so.
One may thus determine the central theme of this sutra: "The Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the foremost of the myriad practices of all bodhisattvas" constitutes one phrase.

Bodhisattvas are those who exist within the state of cause; their names are manifold. If even a single bodhisattva is already endowed with these various practices, how much more so must be the cultivation undertaken by all bodhisattvas?
When ancient masters explained this title, they cited the fifty-seven stages from the eighth fascicle [of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*] as the progression from cause.

It is not erroneous to say that the ultimate fruit corresponds to the myriad practices (*saṃskāra*). However, "stages" (*bhūmi*) refer to what is realized (*prāpti*), while "practices" refer to the process of advancing toward it.

How could the stages themselves directly correspond to the practices? To correspond to the practices, one must point to the cultivation undertaken at the time of intending to enter a stage and at the time of having already entered it;

this accords with the intent of the sūtra. Furthermore, this sūtra investigates the mind and discriminates the views regarding the five aggregates (*skandha*), the three categories (*dhātu*), the seven elements (*dhātu*), and all other phenomena.

"O Yuantong, by practicing in reliance upon this, one fulfills all the ritual methods of a Bodhisattva. Therefore, within the *Prajñāpāramitā*, it is described as the Bodhisattva’s practice throughout kalpas;
in this present sutra, it is termed the 'Ten Thousand Practices of Śūraṅgama. As the sutra says, 'The King of Śūraṅgama is fully endowed with the ten thousand practices.
Based on this, one should take the Great Śūraṅgama Samādhi as the general [principle] and the ten thousand practices as the particulars. Regarding the general samādhi:
One who possesses these distinct qualities is designated as a "King. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Śūraṃgama" means that all matters are completed; "Vijaya" (translated as "Yan") means firmness.
Because all things are ultimately brought to completion and one attains firmness, it is named Śūraṃgama-vijaya. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Śūraṃgama" is called "Jianxiang" (Strong Appearance) in the Qin language. It refers to the discerning knowledge of the various characteristics, numbers, depths, and shallowness of all samādhis, just like a great general.
He knows the number and strength of all military forces. When a Bodhisattva attains this samādhi, no afflictions or the like can destroy him.
It is like the wheel-turning king (cakravartin), whose treasure of the military commander reaches every place such that none dare to cause destruction.

Therefore, it is also translated as "the completion of the task. This may encompass the application of the present sutra. The aforementioned "Tathāgata" refers to the person; "the secret causes," etc., refer to the practice.

The Dharma. The Bodhisattva is the person; the myriad practices and so forth are the Dharma. Although these are what is expounded in the Exoteric Teachings, how could this meaning not also be present within the Secret Mantras?
Question: Formerly, Gushan explained the title of the scripture as being "named by possessing the three," yet Tongzhou refuted this.
"Now, how does this fully embody the meaning of the three chapters? Answer: The *Miaoxuan* states: "The 'Explanation of Names' provides a general discussion of the three dharmas;

the 'Body, Teaching, and Function' opens up and correlates these with the three dharmas. Upon examining the title of the present *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, one now knows that the ancient claim that the 'Explanation of Names' is general while the [subsequent] three chapters are specific is indeed based on reality.
However, "Great Buddha-Topknot" belongs to the Body (*tǐ*), and "Secret Cause, Cultivation, and Realization" constitutes the Teaching (*zōng*). Regarding the Function (*yòng*)... [text continues].

The meanings are all consistent. However, while the myriad practices of a Bodhisattva are the phenomena within the cause, they seem more appropriately to belong to the "thesis" (zhòng) rather than the "function" (yòng).

Yet, the *Shiqian* (Explanatory Notes), in its commentary on the "Ten Profound Subtleties" (*Xuanyi*), states: "The object is the essence; it is the Dharmakāya. Wisdom and practice are the thesis; they are the function.

According to that text, the "subtlety of practice" is the function; how then can the myriad practices of a Bodhisattva not be considered a function? [This applies to] both the general and the specific.
This explanation leaves no room for further doubt.

Next, the general name is explained. "Sūtra" (經) is glossed as "dharma" (法) and "constant" (常). It is called "dharma" because, by means of this verbal expression, it elucidates the nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), thereby causing sentient beings to give rise to understanding.
It is called "constant" because all Buddhas alike deliver such teachings. There is also a translation [for "sūtra"]:...
The absence of a corresponding term in other languages is as explained in the *Myōgen* (The Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra).

This concludes the section on "Explaining the Name" (*shimei*). Second, regarding the "Discerning the Substance" (*benti*): this sūtra takes the wondrous True Suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha as its substance.

If one relies on the title of the sūtra, it takes the "Great Buddha-Crown" (*Daibutsuchō*) as its substance. Generally, Hīnayāna sūtras possess three seals (*mudrā*), whereas Mahāyāna possesses only one seal; this "seal" refers to—

This is the essence. In the Hīnayāna, it is taught that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are distinct. Within saṃsāra, the seal of impermanence (*anityatā*) is the first and the seal of non-self (*anātman*) is the last;
these two seals are used to characterize saṃsāra. Nirvāṇa, however, employs only the single seal of tranquility (*śānti*). Therefore, all three are required.
When these three dharmas are present, one knows they are the Buddha’s teaching, and by practicing them, one attains the Way. Without the three seals of dharma, [it is not].
This is the teaching of Māra; therefore, it takes the three dharmas as its essence. In the Mahāyāna, birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, and nirvāṇa is itself birth-and-death;
they are non-dual and without distinction, being only the one true reality, which is called the Seal of the True Reality (bhūtatathatāmudrā). The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* says:

"Non-characteristic, non-non-characteristic, and non-non-characteristic—this is called the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The commentary explains: "Non-characteristic" means the absence of the characteristics of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

"Non-characteristic" [in the second instance] means the absence of the characteristic of nirvāṇa. Furthermore, it says "non-non-characteristic and non-characteristic," meaning that even the characteristic of non-nirvāṇa is itself without characteristic.
Now, the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa [Samādhi] is realized by virtue of this principle of the true characteristic, thereby achieving the state of "no-seeing."
The *uṣṇīṣa* (crown protuberance) is one of the thirty-two marks of a Great Being. When its essence is investigated, it is the reality-mark (*tathatā*) and the Dharma-body;
for this reason, it is specifically called the "Great Buddha-uṣṇīṣa. Although this essence is inherently possessed by all sentient beings, it is realized only by a Buddha. As the *Miaoxuan* states:
Is it not the case that taking what the Buddha perceived as the primary substance (*tattva*) of this present sutra is indeed correct?

Furthermore, the reason for taking the *Tathāgatagarbha* nature [as the substance] is that it is the ultimate destination of the text’s meaning and the grand theme of the entire scripture; since it corresponds to the meaning of "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" in the title, it is designated as the substance.
What is meant by "the ultimate destination of the text’s meaning"? The sutra clarifies the various *samādhis*, stating in the text: "First..."
All fleeting, dusty, and illusory manifestations arise at the very place they appear and perish at the very place they are;

these illusory and false appearances are called "characteristics," yet their nature is truly the essence of wondrous, enlightened clarity. Thus it is with the five aggregates and six sense bases, from the twelve entrances to the eighteen realms:

through the conjunction of causes and conditions there is illusory birth, and through the separation of causes and conditions there is what is illusorily termed "extinction. This is distinct [from ultimate reality].

They were unable to know that birth and extinction, going and coming, are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha—the eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, and all-pervading nature of the wondrous True Suchness (*tathatā*).
It is here that the name "Tathāgata-garbha-nature" first appears. However, the World-Honored One’s speaking of it was by no means arbitrary;

rather, he necessarily proceeded through three rounds of affirmation and negation before clarifying its meaning. "Practice" (*xing*) refers to progression, meaning the progressive clarification of perfect completeness.

This is the teaching. What is meant by "denial" (fǒu)? It refers to the distinct application of the inverted and the circular [methods]. What is meant by the three successive stages of advancement and denial?
Following the scripture’s investigation of the mind at seven locations, Ānanda doubted that the mind had no substance.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause Ānanda and the great assembly to enter the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), rubbed the crown of Ānanda’s head while seated upon the lion throne.
He addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata has always taught that all phenomena which arise are manifested solely by the mind.

All causes and effects, as well as the atoms of the world-system, take their substance from the mind. This first round of instruction on 'Mind-Only' is the further clarification of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao)."
However, in order for Ānanda to recognize that mind, one must first dispel the external objects (*pūrvadhātu*) to reveal the nature of seeing alone.

Thus, there are such statements as: "The external objects are themselves dark; what deficiency could there be in seeing? and so on, up to: "A lamp can manifest color, but the seeing that perceives it is the eye, not the lamp.
The eye can manifest color, but the nature of seeing that perceives it is the mind, not the eye. (End of the first fascicle)

There is the responsibility for those with a nature-bound mind who lose their way and mistake external objects for themselves. The "Chapter on King Ambarīṣa" states: "Though your face may be wrinkled, this essence of seeing has never been wrinkled.
That which wrinkles is subject to change; that which does not wrinkle is not subject to change. That which changes undergoes extinction;
that which is unchanging is fundamentally without birth or death. As indicated by the above scriptural passage, this constitutes the first instance of distinguishing the false to clarify the true.
The reason the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is in a state of stagnation is that if one does not understand "mind-only," the Perfect School cannot be established;

and if one does not discern false conditions, the true mind will not manifest. Therefore, there is a profound reason for selecting [the true] from amidst the adventitious dust and for repeatedly engaging in the debate between the subject and emptiness.
First, when it is clarified that all phenomena are mind-only, all phenomena are eternal—is this not the Perfect? Next, the subject...
The guest replies: "To distinguish between the arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing as two entirely separate paths—is this not a distinction?

Yet to claim that the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is purely a teaching of the Perfect (Cakra) Vehicle is surely erroneous. [The Master says: "Using the distinct [teaching] as a skillful means for entering the Perfect is precisely what the Sūtra means by the phrase 'the foremost skillful means.
Next, Ānanda again clings to the view that the non-arising-and-non-ceasing nature of seeing and hearing is..."
Regarding the true nature, when the Buddha questioned them about the locus of their delusions, they were utterly bewildered and did not know.

The Buddha, arising in great compassion, uttered the ocean-tide voice to proclaim universally to the assembled multitude: "The various conditions of form and mind, as well as all phenomena that serve as objects for the mental factors, are manifested solely by the mind.
Your bodies and your minds are all objects manifested within the wondrously luminous, true essence of the wondrous mind. This points directly to the truth.

It is said that the retribution is solely the true mind. Furthermore, it states: "The physical body, extending outward to the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth—all are objects within the wondrously luminous true mind.
This refers collectively to the fact that the environment-retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*) is also solely the true mind. The Sūtra establishes a simile and concludes with a reproof, saying:

It is like discarding hundreds of thousands of vast, clear oceans and instead identifying with the body of a single floating bubble, claiming it to be the entire tide and exhausting the whole expanse of the sea.
You all are people who are doubly deluded; the Tathāgata calls you objects of compassion.
The above scriptural passage constitutes the second instance of advancing the clarification of "Mind-Only. The preceding first instance was merely the establishment of the thesis;

now, this second instance extensively elucidates the perfect intent. However, because Ānanda had personally presented what he had realized and yet still relied upon the conditioned mind in his respectful gaze, the Buddha employed the metaphor of the finger pointing at the moon and the host and guest to once again clarify the nature of seeing, stating: "Luminosity returns..."

The sun returns to the dark; the black moon returns to the light; the thoroughfare returns to the door and window; the obstruction returns to the wall and house; discrimination returns to its conditions; the stubborn void returns to emptiness;

the turbid dust returns to the particles; the clear brightness returns to the clearing sky. Among these eight kinds of things you perceive, to whom should the luminous nature of your seeing itself return?
That which can return naturally is not you. As for that which does not return to anything else—who is it but you? (From the later passage)

Furthermore, it is said that while categories of things naturally possess distinctions, the seeing-nature (dṛṣṭi-svabhāva) has no difference. It is also said: "If you do not see the ground of my 'not-seeing,' then it would naturally not be a thing;

how could it not be yours? Now, according to what was stated in the preceding sutra, whether [the objects] are the support or the supported, they are all things within the wondrously luminous true mind.
Yet now, these categories of things are again set aside to uniquely reveal the true seeing. This is the... [first chapter].
The second repetition clarifies the distinction regarding the Perfect [Teaching]. For if the mind-only principle were not reiterated, the profound purport of the Perfect would not be fully expressed;
and if the non-retrogressive vision of the nature were not clarified, delusive conditions would not be eliminated. Thus, these serve as the negations for the Perfect Teaching.

May Ānanda’s knot of doubt be suddenly resolved, so that through these skillful means he may enter the Perfect School. Ānanda again doubted that the faculty of sight could expand and contract; the Buddha rebuked him.

It is said that all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been deluded by taking themselves to be objects and have thus lost their original mind, allowing themselves to be turned by external things.

For this reason, within these circumstances, they perceive the great as small. If one can instead turn objects [to serve the self], then one will be identical to the Tathāgata, with body and mind perfectly luminous and unmoving within the site of enlightenment, able to universally contain the worlds of the ten directions upon the tip of a single hair. This is the third.

The first two sections advance to clarify the principle of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanli*). Clarifying the Perfect Teaching by advancing refers to the discourse on "Mind-Only" (*weixin*); clarifying the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) by retreating refers to the discourse on "seeing one's nature" (*jianxing*).
Now, in this third section, we directly take "seeing one's nature" as the basis to conclude with and return to the principle of the Perfect Teaching.

Furthermore, while the previous discussion of Mind-Only was still applicable to the causal stage (*yin*), the present discussion of the hair swallowing the mustard seed and the inclusion [of the world] pertains directly to the manifestation of the fruit-virtue (*guode*). This continues until the end...
The text states: "This seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi;
how could there be 'is' or 'is not' within them? This also uses the nature of seeing to lead back to the Perfect [Dharma].
Next, Ānanda again asks about natural causes and conditions, and the Tathāgata refutes each one in turn, even saying: "When you see light, the seeing is not the light; when you see darkness..."
When seeing what is not dark, that seeing is not darkness; when seeing emptiness, that seeing is not emptiness; when seeing obstruction, that seeing is not obstruction.
As stated in the Sūtra, it is clear that the nature of seeing is detached from external objects. Furthermore, it says: "When seeing the act of seeing, that seeing is not [ordinary] seeing;
even seeing is detached from seeing, such that seeing cannot reach it. As stated in the Sūtra, the nature of seeing is detached from the internal faculties.

This is clear. This third instance clarifies the distinct teaching (biejiao). Previously it was said: "These views and their objects are fundamentally bodhi"—is this not the perfect teaching (yuanjiao)?
Next it was said: "The faculties, objects, light, darkness, space, and obstruction are all not the nature of seeing"—is this not the distinct teaching?

Furthermore, it was shown that both types of false views—the common and the distinct—are [ultimately] the perfect teaching. Thus, it was not until the third demonstration that the perfect teaching was revealed.
In principle, the realm of the Buddha would not manifest; yet, if one does not strictly discern and eliminate false views, the counterfeit faculties will not be removed.
Subsequently, the scripture further refutes both "conjunction" and "non-conjunction" to conclude the three stages of progression and regression.

Only after these three stages does it finally resolve [the teaching] in the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, clarifying all *samādhis*. Why is this so? Because the first three stages employ distinct [methods].
The intent lies in advancing toward the three stages of perfection. The great purport of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) is to clarify that all is but mind.

The substance of the mind is pervasive and perfect, encompassing the worlds of the ten directions; this is precisely the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. "Garbha" (Zang) takes the sense of containing or storing within.

One must first understand the measure of the mind before reaching the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*; only then does it truly manifest its name, following this sequential order of convergence. The subsequent seven [stages] are eternally abiding.
In the "Chapter on Perfect Penetration," it says: "Establishing the Great Perfect Mirror as the Empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Is this not precisely where the purport of the text leads? Why is it said that this is extensively discussed in a single sutra?

Although the sutra reveals at the beginning of its sections on the five aggregates and the three categories the name "the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha," the concluding text subsequently states only that it is fundamentally neither cause nor effect.

Because conditions are not of a spontaneous nature, the meaning has not yet been fully revealed; those who are deluded still maintain that although the name "storehouse" (ālaya) exists, the dharma stored therein has not yet been seen.
Consequently, they request an exposition of the definitive meaning of the Middle Way.

The Tathāgata then demonstrates that the earth, water, fire, and wind, as well as boundless empty space, clear vision, and discriminating consciousness, are all none other than inherent virtues of the nature—this is the demonstration of the inherent completeness of the nature.

This is the Dharma. Now, those who penetrate the mind-only and realize its inherent completeness understand the perfect purport. While the first two fascicles extensively clarify mind-only (*cittamātra*), it is only upon reaching the third fascicle that the inherent completeness of nature (*xingju*) is elucidated.
Thus, mind-only serves as the gateway to the inherent completeness of nature, while the inherent completeness of nature is the ultimate purport of mind-only.

Once the inherent completeness of nature is manifest, the Tathāgatagarbha is revealed; it is only when the audience reaches this point that they finally awaken to the identity of the one and the many.

The essence of all minds universally contains [all phenomena]; thus there is the verse: "To eliminate my inverted thoughts of billions of kalpas, and to attain the Dharmakāya without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

It is clear that this is attained through awakening to the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). However, because the nature is replete with all dharmas, it possesses both the characteristics of being replete and not replete;
therefore, Pūrṇa manifested as one who was deluded, establishing the difficulty of water and fire mutually overcoming each other, while earth and space coexist.

Regarding the doubt concerning pervasiveness: for this reason, the Tathāgata further spoke of the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind as being originally neither water nor fire, extensively clarifying the principle of the Tathāgata-garbha.
To say that "the fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and round mind is in all respects neither [of the ten realms]" is the meaning of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

That "the primordial luminosity of the wondrous mind is in all respects identical with the ten realms" is the purport of the Provisional (*prajñapti*). That "the wondrous luminosity of the mind's origin is detached from both identity and difference" is the meaning of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).

This is not merely the path of "non-identity within identity. Upon reaching this point, the principle of the *tathāgatagarbha* is fully manifested, perfect understanding is awakened, and doubts are almost entirely eliminated.
It is upon this foundation that perfect practice and perfect realization are established. Alas!

The delusions of the people of the world have persisted for a long time. As explained extensively in the third fascicle, the meaning of the "Treasury" (Garbha) is clarified through the doctrine of the inherent nature (prakṛti-sampad).

Yet, commentators of both past and present still claim that water and fire definitely do not exist within the nature; they argue that because their manifestations differ, the nature itself receives the names of the seven elements (mahābhūta).

This master [Zhiyi] did not realize the inherent nature; seeing later passages where it says, "Observing the primordial reality of the nature, it is solely the wondrous enlightenment," he failed to grasp the full significance.

This refers to the statement that the mind of wondrous enlightened clarity was originally neither water nor fire. Thus, you have used the intent of the fourth fascicle to interpret the text of the third fascicle.
You do not realize that the seven elements are merely the single hidden nature (*tathāgatagarbha*); that within this nature, the seven elements are fully present, as is clearly evident in the text.

To bring forth one is to encompass all; it is likewise so for the others. This is the subtle mystery of this self-nature wherein the one and the many mutually contain one another. Otherwise, why would [the Buddha] have said...?
It is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. Furthermore, in the fourth fascicle it says: "The wondrously enlightened, luminous mind was originally neither water nor fire;
why then do you ask about their mutual incompatibility? This passage does not mean that water and fire were originally absent within the nature and only later arose from it.

One should understand that the character "originally" (*xian*) and the character "again" (*fu*) are to be read in contrast. It states that the wondrous mind was already not water or fire—how could it then "again" [become so]?

Question: Regarding those who claim [the elements] are mutually incompatible: since water is not non-water and fire is not non-fire, they call it the "wondrous mind. The commentators are confused and say:
"When [the elements] first exist as nature (*xing*), although there is the nature of water and the nature of fire, there are no phenomenal forms of water or fire;

therefore, there is no mutual suppression or extinction. If one were to say that within nature there is no water or fire at all, this would contradict the principle of the inherent presence of all things (*xingju*). This master says that nature...
Within [the nature], water and fire are necessarily present. Thus, one uses the meaning of the third fascicle to interpret the text of the fourth fascicle.

One should know that the inherent presence of water and fire is precisely not water and fire. Therefore, the ancients said: "The aspect of possessing non-possession is the entire body of reality, which is itself emptiness.
If this wondrous nature possessed even a single dharma that could be apprehended, how could it be called the *tathāgatagarbha* of emptiness? Those who interpret it today...

For example, the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* cites three aspects of the Tathāgatagarbha to explain the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*. However, upon examining the present scripture, there is only the "empty Tathāgatagarbha" (*śūnya-tathāgatagarbha*) and no other two names.
Yet, by establishing this single name alone, its meaning is sufficient. Here, "emptiness" (*śūnya*) is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);

"garbha" (*tathāgatagarbha*) is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); and "Tathāgata" is the middle way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). These three are one, and thus it is called the "empty Tathāgatagarbha. The *Ratnakūṭa* is not... [text truncated]
This sutra is not a minor one. In the seventh fascicle it says: "The wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and detached from all names and marks;

originally there have been no worlds or sentient beings. In the ninth fascicle it says: "Thoroughly investigating the seven realms of existence, they are all states of delusion and the marks of conditioned phenomena;
within the wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind of non-action, they are all like flowers in the sky, fundamentally having nothing to which they adhere. In the tenth fascicle it says: [as above].
"Entering the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment, fulfilling bodhi, and returning to non-attainment"—all these are its meanings.

Therefore, no other passage in this sutra is more extensively discussed than this. As for the title "Great Buddha-Crown," it refers to the markless essence that universally encompasses the dharma-realm;
were it not for this extensive elucidation of the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, how could the meaning of the "Great Buddha-Crown" be revealed? Wondrous!
Xuán said: "The essence (tǐ) is ritual (lǐ). The essence of the sovereign and father is honorable; the essence of the minister and son is humble.
The meaning of that passage indicates that the true mark (shíxiàng) is the sovereign and father, while all phenomena (zhūfǎ) are the ministers and sons.

One should know that the expression 'the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha of the Great Buddha-Crown' refers to the most exalted dharma. Question: "Gushan takes the eternally abiding true mind as the essence; why do you now not [do so]?"

[Question: Is that so? [Answer: The mind is named "following conditions" (*suiyuan*), while its nature is named "unchanging" (*bùbiàn*). One should fully understand that the essence (*tǐ*) consists of the nature of the mind.

Now, following an explanation from the fundamental essence, I shall state the essentials by simply saying "nature. Furthermore, the term "permanently abiding" (*chángzhù*) is precisely the meaning of "treasury" (*zàng*).
Why? As the *Miaoxuan* states: "The Lesser Vehicle’s [attainment] of ash-like cessation lacks the wish-fulfilling jewel body. Based on this text, it is known that...
Only when one possesses a body like a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) can it be called "eternally abiding" (nitya).

This means that from the state of fruition, one manifests bodies of the ten dharma realms (*dharmadhātu*) to preach the Dharma and benefit sentient beings, just as a king of wish-fulfilling jewels rains down treasures according to one's wishes. Since this mind is already fully possessed within the causal stage, it is also called "eternally abiding.
What difference is there between this and the Tathāgatagarbha, which contains all things within itself yet remains without accumulation? Therefore, [the text] merely explains...
The Tibetan name itself speaks of permanence. This concludes the analysis of the essence (*tattva*). Third, as for the primary tenet (*mūla*):

it takes the sublime samādhi of the *Śūraṃgama* as its tenet. If one follows the title of the scripture, it takes "the definitive meaning of the Tathāgata’s secret cause, cultivation, and realization" as its tenet.
"Tenet" (*mūla*) means that which is honored and essential. A scripture having a tenet is like a house having a main beam.
The Pillar. The net has its cords and meshes; it serves as the sovereign of the single thread and the guide for those who practice correctly.
Yet, while it was previously stated that the Great Buddha-Crown (Mahā-uṣṇīṣa) is the most noble principle and its substance is supremely honored, why is the character [“Crown”] now further honored?
One should know that "substance" refers to the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), whereas "tenet" refers to the matters of cultivation and realization. If it were not for the wondrous...
By what means is the essence of the school manifested? The essence constitutes the essence of the school, while the school serves to manifest that essence.

Since the essence also belongs to the school, the school is the essential framework. Within the wondrous samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama*, the three types of cessation-and-contemplation reside within a single mind.
If one can understand this, it is the secret cause. "Cultivation" refers to cultivating this wondrous samādhi; "realization" refers to realizing this wondrous samādhi. Regarding cultivation...
In the *Zhengzhong* (The Proof of the Middle), it is generally stated that the "one among the three" is designated as the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Regarding this sutra, when Ānanda, the primary interlocutor, first requested [instruction on] how the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain Bodhi through the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*, as well as their initial expedient means, commentators from ancient times to the present have offered various interpretations.
Guishan composed an explanation based on the "three types of cessation" (*trividha-śamatha*), stating: "In the Sanskrit language..."
*Śamatha* is translated here as "stopping" (*zhi*). Stopping within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is "stopping that accords with reality" (*tǐzhēn zhǐ*).

*Samādhi* in Sanskrit is translated here as "equipoise" (*děngchí*). Being free from dullness and agitation is called "equilibrium" (*děng*); dwelling the mind on a single object is called "maintenance" (*chí*).

Stopping within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is "stopping that follows conditions through skillful means" (*fāngbiàn suíyuán zhǐ*). *Dhyāna* in Sanskrit is translated here as "meditative concentration" (*jìnglù*). Stopping within the Middle Way is the "supreme [concentration]."
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is precisely the cessation of dualistic conceptualization through tranquility (*śamatha*). *Śūraṅgama* is a general name for *śamatha* and its counterparts;
*śamatha*, etc., are specific designations of *Śūraṅgama*. Ānanda possesses great power of wisdom but little power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Having already reproached himself for his meager learning and limited wisdom, he specifically requested instruction on the Great Samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama*. Wuxing remarked:
"Gushan’s exclusive application of the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) to correspond with the three names [of the samādhis] captures the profound depth of the sūtra.

However, Zizhong used the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* to explain them as the three contemplations (*vipaśyanā*). Indeed, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "All Bodhisattvas are unimpeded and pure..."
Wisdom arises entirely in dependence upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*), namely *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*. Based on this, it is clear that all three are termed "concentration.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "*Śamatha* is ultimate stillness; *samādhi* is correct mindfulness and retention."

The section on the "Clarification of the Counting of Dhyāna" is called the "Threefold Pure Contemplation. Based on this, it is further clarified that all three are designated as contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

In the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, the three names beginning with *śamatha* were previously used to encompass both cessation (*śamatha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); why then should this present sūtra be any different?
The second fascicle states: "At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and the great assembly, was about to expound the Great..."
Regarding the path of sublime practice for various *dhāraṇīs* and *samādhis*, he said to Ānanda: "Though you possess a powerful memory, it merely increases your erudition;
yet regarding the subtle and secret contemplation within *śamatha*, your mind has not yet fully realized it.

The scripture speaks of *śamatha* and also of "subtle and secret contemplation"—is this not precisely the contemplation that is identical with cessation (*śamatha*)? Below, he elucidates the two aspects of identity and difference.
The cultivation of the false view is precisely the subtle and secret contemplation of *śamatha*; it is the prevailing discourse on entering the path of emptiness.

Thus, since *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are both present within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), what cause for doubt could there be? Since this is the case regarding the ultimate truth, it is likewise so for the conventional middle way (*madhyamā-prajñapti*).

Now, *samādhi* is fundamentally translated as "equipoise" (*samā-dhāraṇa*). Since it is free from dullness and agitation, focusing the mind on a single object is precisely the meaning of *śamatha*. — Miaole.
The twenty-ninth fascicle, on the fifty-eighth sheet, states: "Samādhi arises from concentration (samāpatti), while dhāraṇī arises from wisdom (prajñā).

Now, since this sutra speaks of a "great dhāraṇī," how could it not possess contemplative wisdom? From this it may be concluded that within samādhi, both śamatha and vipaśyanā are necessarily present;
and as for the Middle Way of dhyāna, where concentration and wisdom are non-dual, it goes without saying. This concludes the explanation of the names.
Some take [the first term] to mean "cessation" (śamatha) and others take it to mean "contemplation" (vipaśyanā); all such explanations are correct, yet one must not adhere to them exclusively.
Now, it is the correct interpretation that the three names collectively encompass both cessation and contemplation. Furthermore, there is a master who says:

*śamatha* is translated as "cessation," *samādhi* as "contemplation," and *dhyāna* as "the simultaneous inclusion of both cessation and contemplation. While this meaning is indeed unimpeded, upon examining the translations, I have not yet seen...
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, *śamatha* is translated as "stopping" (*zhǐ*) and *vipaśyanā* as "contemplation" (*guān*), while *vīkṣā* refers to "stopping and contemplation" (*zhíguān*).
This sutra also states that within *śamatha*, one employs the *vipaśyanā* of all Tathāgatas;
thus, these names specifically refer to stopping and contemplation. How could one directly take *samādhi* to be contemplation? Examining the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuánjué jīng*), it says:
Śamatha is quiescent like a mirror manifesting all images; samādhi gives rise to illusions like sprouts gradually growing;

dhyāna is solely cessation, like the hollows within a vessel. According to the text of the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (Yuánjué jīng), these three names refer precisely to emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
Now, when these three dharmas are present within a single mind, they are then called "wondrous. As it says in the *Zhōngjì*: "The ancients..."

Those who have come to explain this sutra originally did not employ the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) to divide the sections. It was only in recent times that the textual divisions were first opened up according to the three contemplations, for which there are two explanations.

The first is as found in Jiaoguang’s *Zhengmai*, which classifies the first three and a half fascicles of the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* as the principle of the *śamatha* of essential concentration (*svabhāva-samādhi*).
From the section beginning with "Requesting Entry into the Flowered Hall" until before the explanation of the mantra, it classifies [the text] as the third [contemplation].
Ma, the subsequent sections of the scripture are collectively termed *dhyāna*. This statement is a great error. Why? Because at the beginning of the "Seven Investigations," it says:
"There is a *samādhi* named Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which is fully endowed with the myriad practices.

Furthermore, in the second fascicle, regarding the five aggregates and the three categories, it names them "the various *samādhis*, the wondrous path of practice. Yet you categorize these all as *śamatha*. This is incorrect.

Is this interpretation tenable? That [opponent] takes exception to the fact that the name "samādhi" appears at the beginning of the seven inquiries, and thus provides a forced explanation, claiming it is merely a temporary designation.
However, since this section is not like the other sections, one cannot rely on it as a universal rule.

Second, the masters of the South regard the passages concerning the inquiry into the mind and the examination of vision as *śamatha*, while they consider the sections from the five aggregates onward to be various forms of *samādhi*. Seven...

Master Daizhi’s textual analysis categorizes this as *dhyāna* (meditative concentration), and Master Youxi’s analysis is likewise. This accords with the intent of the Tathāgata’s three successive contemplations (*tri-krama-vipaśyanā*).

However, since the text itself explicitly states at the beginning of the section on "Discerning the Views" (*vibhaṅga-darśana*) that one must first seek the path of *śamatha*, what further doubt could there be?
Furthermore, the opening text of the "Seven Investigations" (*sapta-praśna*) states, "There is *samādhi*," yet commentators universally judge this to be *śamatha*.
Is this not reasonable? It is simply because various masters have not skillfully utilized the text of the *Ārya-śrī-mālā-sūtra* that their structural divisions (kē) do not accord with it.
Once one grasps the intent of the *Śrīmālā*, it becomes perfectly clear and free of doubt. The first fascicle of the *Śrīmālā*, on the fifth sheet, states:

"The contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional is also called the contemplation of the two truths; the contemplation of emerging from emptiness into the conventional is also called the contemplation of equality. These two contemplations serve as the skillful means."

One attains entry into the contemplation of the Middle Way and the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya). With each thought-moment extinguished, one naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
Since this scriptural passage clearly elucidates the sequential threefold contemplation (*krama-tri-vipaśyanā*), why not cite it to categorize the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*?

It is because the *samādhi* [of the *Śūraṅgama*] belongs to the provisional category of "illusion-like" (*māyopama*); there is no doubt regarding this meaning. As the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*圆觉经*) states: "The arising of *samādhi*..."

It is an illusion. The present sutra also speaks of the "illusion-like samādhi" (yathā-māyopama-samādhi). Thus, the basis for taking samādhi as a provisional contemplation (jaguān) is derived from these two sutras;
it is not a mere speculative assertion. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Kāla is real time, while samaya is provisional time.
According to this passage from the *Śāstra*, it is also evident that *samādhi* is provisional. Therefore, we know that the present sutra investigates the mind and distinguishes [its nature].
It is appropriate that "seeing" (dṛṣṭi) belongs to the contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā). Yet, at the beginning of the "Seven Investigations," it is stated that there is samādhi;

and at the outset of the analysis of seeing, one requests instruction on the path of śamatha—namely, the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional (saṃvṛti-praveśa-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā). Does this not mean that the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* says:

"Contemplating the conventional is the means for entering emptiness, and emptiness is realized through that means"? Furthermore, does this not accord with the established categories [of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*] and the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*?

If one synthesizes these scriptures, there should be no further confusion. However, entering emptiness from the conventional is not the primary intent; rather, this scripture elucidates both the Perfect (Yuan) and the Distinct (Bie) teachings.

The Perfect teaching is the primary intent, while the Distinct is a secondary intent. When a beginner in the Perfect Teaching enters from the conventional, they simultaneously possess the three truths.

As the *Miaoxuan* states: "When the illusion of view-and-thought is destroyed, the truth of reality (zhen-di) is manifested as an illusion; when the illusion of ignorance is destroyed, the truth of conventionality (su-di) is manifested as an illusion."

Accomplished. Within the breaking of the illusion of ignorance, the illusion of the Middle Way is accomplished. The present text is likewise so. To penetrate these provisional phenomena, the three contemplations are fully present, and thus the myriad practices are complete.
Therefore, following the passage on *samādhi*, it says: "Named the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, fully endowed with the myriad practices. This is the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching].
If a person of the Separate Teaching cultivates the contemplation of entering emptiness from the provisional, the seven locations...

The investigation of the mind is precisely at the stage of following the provisional; it is only when one reaches the subsequent request for instruction on the path of *śamatha* that one enters into emptiness.

Now, differentiation is itself distinctness, while the fusion of distinctions is itself perfection. The Tathāgata established his thesis based on the principle of perfection, whereas Ānanda formulated his question according to the expedient means of distinction.

Thus, perfection and distinction do not obstruct one another; nor is there anything that does not manifest perfection through distinction, nor anything that does not manifest distinction through perfection.
Rong’s distinction between dharmas should be thus. In the preceding "Chapter on Substance," three stages of progress and non-progress were clarified;
the very foundation of this progress and non-progress lies precisely here. Why do people today merely observe the literal text without examining its underlying meaning?

Some claim that wherever the various sutras and śāstras indicate the method for practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, it is all termed *samādhi*; therefore, *samādhi* is a general name, while *Śūraṅgama* is... [a specific one].

"Yan" (Strictness) is a specific designation; that explanation is indeed correct. However, the reason *samādhi* is used as a general term is precisely because, by concentrating the mind on a single object, there is nothing it cannot accomplish;
thus, both the sutras and the śāstras employ this name. Since it concentrates on a single object, is it not metaphorical?
This being so, the same principle applies to the initial contemplation within the three successive contemplations, and likewise to the emergence from emptiness into the provisional.
However, the passage previously cited—"about to expound the sublime path of practice for all samādhis"—is precisely the text in question.
Since one intends to emerge from emptiness into the provisional, it first expounds the subtle and secret contemplation of *śamatha*, and subsequently clarifies the various *samādhis*.
Interpreting it in this way not only accords with the *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng), but also captures the profound essence of the present scripture.
It is also clearly elucidated. Nevertheless, although it contains the intent of the gradual teachings, because its meaning lies in the Perfect [Teaching], it is called "the Path of Sublime Practice.
This means that when one thoroughly penetrates each and every samādhi, there is nothing that is not the perfect contemplation; this is the path for entering Bodhi.

Upon reaching the passage on the "Seven Great Elements" in the third fascicle, the explanation is given according to the gradual approach, which is the same as the two contemplations in the *Ratnavyūha-sūtra* (瓔珞經) serving as the skillful means for attainment.

[The text] enters into the Middle Way of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Question: If one follows the sequential [teaching], the emptiness and the provisional were clarified previously, and at this point it would be appropriate to clarify the Middle Way.
If one relies on the perfect and sudden [teaching], the Middle Way has already been clarified previously; why then is there a request for the Middle Way here? Answer:

The Tathāgata established his doctrine by combining the perfect with the distinct. Ānanda’s questions mostly concern the distinct teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*). This is for the purpose of establishing the initial [stage].
This is due to the use of skillful means (*upāya*). However, that which is being requested here is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the Middle Way.

This means that while the preceding [teachings] were not without the Middle Way, they merely clarified "mind-only" (*cittamātra*) and had not yet clarified the inherent nature (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*). Now, it is necessary to clarify the seven great aspects of the inherent nature; only then is it the definitive meaning.

Furthermore, the simultaneous rejection of both "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) and "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) constitutes the meaning of the Middle Way's dual negation (*ubhayanirodha*); one must further clarify the seven aspects of the inherent nature.

When the Great [Teachings] advance to illuminate all things exhaustively, only then is it the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Therefore, it is after the text on the Seven Great Elements that the definitive meaning is fully revealed.

Ānanda and the great assembly then spoke verses in praise of the Buddha. Question: Regarding the sequence of the Three Truths, one first [contemplates] emptiness, then the provisional (*upāya*), and finally the Middle;
why is it not heard that one first contemplates provisional phenomena? Answer: Entering emptiness from the provisional is called "emptiness preceding the provisional. From emptiness, one emerges...
This "provisional" (jia) refers to the provisional that follows emptiness. That the scriptural text is thus is not a matter of mere personal conjecture.
Within the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, the provisional also occupies the foremost position. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), fascicle 21, states: "The three truths have no form and are all invisible;

nevertheless, the provisional dharma can be explained by relying on phenomena. This very provisional dharma is itself emptiness and itself the Middle. The two principles of emptiness and the Middle are non-dual."

According to this passage from the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), is it not the case that the contemplation of the provisional (*jia-guan*) occupies the foremost position? The *Shi bu'er men* (Ten Gates of Non-duality) states:

"Because of illumination, the three thousand [realms] are eternally present; because of cessation, they are naturally empty. Master Jingxi’s use of the term "provisional" here likewise places it at the forefront. The "three thousand" refers precisely to the phenomena of the provisional.
In Master Miaole’s commentary on the *Wan er qian ren ju guan xin wen* (The Text on the Contemplation of Mind by the Twelve Thousand People) within the sutra, he says: "As for the objective realm..."

If we provisionally allow for numbers at the level of conventional designation (*prajñapti*), where would those numbers exist within emptiness (*śūnyatā*)? Nevertheless, one must rely upon the conventional to establish emptiness;
contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is likewise so. Thus, the opening of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* refers to *samādhi* as relying upon the conventional to establish emptiness.
One should know that the three contemplations ultimately reside within a single mind without distinction of before or after, yet they are employed as contemplative practices.

At that time, one must necessarily rely upon provisional phenomena (*prajñapti*) to give rise [to realization]. If one does not contemplate the provisional, by what means could one enter the principle of emptiness?
Now, the first three fascicles of this sutra discuss the non-sequential according to the sequential; every section is perfect and distinct, yet they are explained together.

The underlying intent lies in the Perfect [Teaching], wherein the One Mind and the Three Truths are non-dual. How can an interpreter fail to grasp the Real while losing the Provisional, or grasp the Real while losing the Provisional?

Yes. In the fourth fascicle, the dialogue between Pūrṇa and the Buddha thoroughly eliminates subtle delusions and extensively elucidates the principle of the Tathāgatagarbha, concluding by revealing the perfect meaning previously established.
By examining this dialogue, one knows that the Buddha’s intention lies solely in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong).

All the assemblies on the Perfect Penetrations of the Sages are the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama; the sixty stages of the sages are none other than the wondrous realization of the One Mind through the three types of cessation (san-zhi).

Perfect penetration is not without partiality or inferiority; when these are brought into accord with the Perfect [Teaching], they all become perfect. Therefore it is said that among their respective practices there is truly no superiority or inferiority.

Although the stages of the sages do not belong to the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*), the Perfect is elucidated by borrowing from the Separate; thus, in order to ascend to the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), one further establishes the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*).
Vimalakīrti said: "Wisdom accompanied by skillful means is liberation; wisdom devoid of skillful means is bondage. The present sutra possesses this wisdom with skillful means.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of two birds flying together; does the present sutra not embody the principle of these two flying together?

Furthermore, in the subsequent extensive examination within the section on the "Māra of the Aggregates," all three names appear, as when it says: "The ten kinds of *dhyāna*..."—this refers to [the faults] of *dhyāna*.

The term "cessation" (śamatha) here encompasses the other two [aspects of] cessation. Furthermore, it is said that when those good sons, while practicing samādhi and śamatha, reach the exhaustion of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), this necessarily implies that the two types of cessation encompass dhyāna.
Just as with the primary śamatha and vipaśyanā, so it is for all subsequent mental states;

they are each the three truths and each the three contemplations (vipaśyanā). If this is true for the primary contemplation of a single mind, it is likewise true for the sequential contemplation that brings about realization.

Therefore, the three names—*śamatha*, *vipaśyanā*, and so forth—appear interchangeably throughout the sūtras, each possessing its own specific meaning. How can one simply claim that mentioning one necessarily implies all three? Question:

Regarding the central tenet (*siddhānta*) of this sūtra, does it reside primarily in the cause (*hetu*) or primarily in the fruit (*phala*)? Answer: The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* take the cause as their central tenet;
the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* takes the fruit as its central tenet. Since the present [text] speaks of the "secret cause" (*guhyahetu*) and its cultivation and realization...
The meaning [of this teaching] takes both cause and effect as its thesis, yet its primary intent lies in the cause. For example, the initial request speaks of the "initial expedient means";
the second fascicle states that those who are not yet beyond training do not vaguely know the beginning and end of this meaning; and the fourth fascicle requests entry into the jeweled house.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas in the assembly, inspired them to resolve upon bodhicitta. They had not yet...

Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings in the Dharma-ending age, [the Buddha] opened the path of wondrous cultivation of the Unsurpassed Vehicle. The Verse on Discerning the Perfect Penetration (*Vyavaccheda-gāthā*) states:
"When those of initial resolve enter samādhi, their speed varies and is not uniform. Furthermore, at the beginning of the passage on discerning the demons of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), it says:
"You who are of the stage of learning—pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—who today turn your minds toward Great Bodhi and the unsurpassed, wondrous awakening... [The *Sūtra* continues.]
The conclusion states that both those who have first resolved their minds and the powerful spirits rejoice greatly.
As these various passages all instruct beginners, it is clear that one should take the realization of the causal mind within the fruit as the primary principle. Question:
Why not adopt the ear-faculty of Avalokiteśvara to establish the method for practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*? Answer: The expedient means of the practice gate lies in the ear.
Regarding the "Root": it is now explained throughout this section as the three types of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Regarding the fourth, the "Function" (*vṛtti*): according to this sutra, its function is to sever craving and distance oneself from worldly dust.

However, if one relies on the title of the sutra, its function is the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the foremost of the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas. Examining the *Xuánqiān* (Profound Commentary), the function is divided into two kinds: first, the function according to the specific school (*zōngjiā*).

There is the "function" (yòng) of the House of Function (yòngjiā), and the "function" of the House of Principle (zōngjiā) pertains to one's own practice (*xing*). This refers to what is called "wisdom-virtue as the principle" (*zhìdé wéi zōng*) and "cessation-virtue as the function" (*duàndé wéi yòng*).

The "function" of the House of Function pertains to adapting to the capacities of beings (*dòujī*). This refers to what is called "transforming others," wherein both wisdom and cessation are taken as the function.
Now, is it not the case that the "Ten Thousand Practices of Śūraṅgama" mentioned in the title refer to the function of the House of Principle? [The] Bodhisattva...

Taking the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) as the primary cultivation and the myriad practices as auxiliary functions, yet further adopting the severance of craving and distancing from dust represents the function of the "household" [the conventional].
Indeed, while the essence and principle are profound and subtle, the function should be expressed in shallow terms while its meaning remains deep.
